• AN EMPTY NEST. BY MARY A. BARR. A grave old man and a maiden fair Walked together at early morn; The thrushes up in the clear cool air Sang to the farmer planting his corn. And, ohl how sweet was the fresh-turned mould! Andtoh, how fair were the budding trees! For daisy's silver and daffodil's gold Were full of the happy honey-bees. "Ab, look! there's an empty nest," she said; " And I wonder where sing the last year's birds?" Then the old man quickly raised his head, Though scarcely he noted her musing words ; He tore the nest from the swaying tree, He flung to the winds its moss and hay, And said, "When an empty nest you see, Be sure you throw it far away." . "But why?" she asked, with a sorrowing face— . "Why may not the pretty home abide?" "Because," he answered, "'twill be a place In which the worm aud the slug will hide. Last year 'twas fair enough in its way— It was full of love, and merry with song; But days that are gone must not spoil to-day, Nor dead joys do the living joys wrong." The in,iiden heard with a thoughtful face Her firk false love had gone far away— And she thought, Is my heart become a place' For anger and grief and hate to stay? Down, heart, with thy sad, forsaken nest! Fling far thy selfish and idle pain; The love that is ours is always the best: And she went with a smile to her work again. THE SHIP OF DREAMS. When silent lies the sleeping town In its profoundest rest, There is a ship conles!salling down Upon the River's breast. Wide-winged as that enchanted swan, She saileth through the night, And purple grows the gloom upon The magic of her flight. The barque she bears no mortal name, No crew of mortal mould, Ulysses ship of song and flame, Of cedar wood and gold!
She hath Ulysses by her helm, As in the olden time; This ship ot a diviner realm, And of a fairer clime.
TAG,

TWE SHIP QF DEATH. When silent lies the sleeping town Unknown to human ken, Another ship goes sailing down, Bearing the souls of Men. She is the ship of shadowy mist, Of mist and mournful grey; There is no gloom of amethyst About her pallid way.

• But sometimes when the dusky tide Bath tilled the -widening stream, That wan and shadowy ship will glide • By the ship of song and dream. Whereon the watchers dimly know • 4 A terror in the dark, A pallor; but a fading glow Flushes the shadovry barque! ' —Longman's Maga:ins. MAY KENDALL.

THE ART OF EXPLOITING. Sir,—There is little doubt that before long the eves of the people will be opened by the great proficiency shown in what 1 must call the art of exploiting. To exploit is to achieve semething. In the matters to which I am going to refer, the something actieved is the wholesale robbery of the people. When Lord Randolph gave his reasons for leaving the Government, be stated amongst other things in the way of economy, that whatever monies we did spend ought to be spent in as efficient a manner as possible, giving es examples, the unseaworthiness of our ironclads, the j im- ming of cartridges and the doubling up of swords and bayonets. Pince ;his speech was given for the edification . of his Tory friends, we have had further startling announce- ments to the effect that our marines are provided with cut- lasses that will bend like seft iron, and that the most noted firm of cartridge makers lose an order in consequence of be- ing a day late with their tender. I say nothing of the further rumours that the Germans, whose especial privi- lege seems to be the draining of English wealth, can run away with our mail contracts, and get hold of the orders for supplying powder and shot for the Britieh army. It might seem invidious to make references to these small matters, as ,we happen to have a Tory Government in power (?) whose strong point has always been their financial and economical policy. Yet one cannot shut one's eyes to the fact that somehow or other an immense amount of money is spent, and still we are nevetein a satisfactory position with out army and navy. Why is this? Is it because we have not I a sufficient nu.nber ef public spirited men? Lord Randolph i said it regnired "the sacrifice of a Chancellor of the Ex- chequer." I think he was right, nay, I think he might have said a dozen, and then have been within the mark. Why is this? Carlyle gave the answer, "because we are artly fools." Sitlit requires a man to make a martyr of himself, to risk prosecution for libel, as Mr. Ellis Lever has done, be- fore the people will believe that they are robbed daily and hourly by those •• Devils who would pal angels out, heaven. Provided they conld reach thorn t, I am reminded sir, that the art of exploiting the people loan old one. Cobbett in hie "Two-peony Trash" revels iii exposil4l the rich ones of his time, those "Good Chris- tians who sate still in easy chair and dam'd the general world for standing up." I find him quoting from a speech of the great Lord Chatham made in the House of Lords on the 22nd of November, 1770. It might be applied to-day as, Sitting for gas managers and Government contractors:— "There is a set of men, my lords, in the city of London, who are known to live in riot and luxury upon the plunder of the ignorant, the innocent and the tideless ; upon that Part of the community which stands most in need of, and lii it list deserves, the care and protection of the leei,lature. To me, my lords, whether they be roi:•erable jobbers of 'Change Alley, or the lofty Asiatic plunderers of Leaden- hall-street, they are all equally detestable. I care but little ine bother a man walks on foot, or is drawn by eight horses Of si7.i. horses; if his luxury be supported by the plunder of bis country I despise andrdetest hint. lete lords. while I had the honour of serving his Majesty. I never ventured to look at the treasury but at a distance : it is a business I am unfit for, and to which I could never have submitted. The little I know of it has not served to raise my opinion of wbat is vulgarly called the monied interest.' I mean that bloodsucker, that muck worm that calls itself the *friend of Government'; that pretends to serve this or that admirals-

STA.RIIING STATISTICS. • The country has been horrified at the recent terrible die- I aster in a theatre in Spitalfields, whereby seventeen persons lost theit lives. This sad calamity carried terror because it
was sudden and appalling, bat bad the same disastrous re-
• • quits to life and limb come silently, they would have been

unnoticed, not only by the public of the United Kingdom, but also by the .very' community in which they occurred. Fatal events of a far worse character are taking place con- stantly, but they attract no attention, not would they, did not the Bureau of Vital Statistics bring them to our notice. Figures do not lie," whatever else may be uncertain, and the report on the deaths of this country is a startling com- ment on halite. Dtiriag the past year the enormous increase of certain maladies is simply appalling.. While the total number of deaths has diminished, and the death-rate of most diseases has decreased, still it is fee greater in one or two serious disorders than was ever before known. More people died in the United Kingdom in wit from diseases of the kidneys than I roped iphtheria, small-pox, and typhoid fever combined. Thil scarcely seems passible, but it is true, and when it is remembered that less than one-third of the actual deaths f MIA Bright's Disease are really reported as such, the ravages of the malady can be partially understood. The immediate query which every reader will snake on such a revelation of facts is. What daises this incrhase? This is a difficult question to answer. The nature of the cllniate, the habits of life, the adulteration of fond and liquors, all un- doubtedly contribute, but no immediate cause can be cer- tainly assigned. •Often be;ore the victim knows it the dis- cease has begun. Its approaches are se stealthy and its symptoms so obscure, that tney cannot be definitely forseen. and are only known by their effects. Any kidney 'disease,' however slight, is the first stage of Bright's Disease, and it 1 Is seldom that kidney disorders can be detected. They do not have any certain symptoms. Mysterious weakness and unusual appetite, periodical headaches, occasional nausea uncertain pains, 1-rss of vigour, lack of nerve power, irregu-9 lafity of the heart' disordered daily habits, imperfect diges- tion ; all these, sod many other symptoms, are the indica- tions of kidney dirprders, even thougn there may be no . pain in the region of the krdneys, or in that portion of the body. The serious nature of these troubles may be under- stood by the fact that Bright's Disease is as certain to follow I disease of the kidneys as decomposition follows death. The alarming increase of kidney diseases their insidious beginnings atid frightful endings, and the acknowledged in- ability of physicians to auccessfuily cope with them, may well awaken the greatest dread of anyone who has the (slightest symptoms. It is fortunate, however, that the surest relief is often found where, possibly least expected, and that a here is a specific for the fatalities above described we have come to fully believe. THE LANGLFY Blip-LARY.

The large party assembled as usual at Langley Towers to celebrate in approved fashion the appreaching Ist of September were all collected one night after dinner in the drawing-room, when the conversation, hither rather languid, chanced to turn on a burglary that had lately taken place in the neighbourhood. Every one at once seized on the topic, and proceeded to relate more or less irrelevant, but all alike ghastly, stories of farneus temg- laries and robberies, till suddenly Miss Cecil Clifford, a cousin of Lady Langley's, a very pretty girl and an heiress to boot, who had hitherto taken no part in the talk, looked up suddenly, and said : " I do wish you would not all discuss such horrors! How do you expect us to sleep quietly in our beds if you will insist on retailing such frightful stories, especially as those wretches who broke into Colston Park are still at large ? I feel as if I shoUld find a burglar in my room, to-night, so if 4 should rouse the house with a false' alarm, don't blame me l" "I think r should 'die if I were to wake and see one in my room I" exclaimed little Lady Langley, shrugging her pretty white shoulder in not wholly affeeted fright. IRE EUROPEAN SITUATION.-HOPEFUL PROSPEOT.—CONTINENTAL PREPARA- TIONS. 1ii"214, SATURDAY.-The expected decree prohibiting the export of horses from Austria-Hungary, is gazetted ba-daY. It will come into force from the date of reaching the various custom houses on the frontier. 11011 E. SUNDAY Nroirr.-The Cecietary for Foreign Affairs, Count di Robilant, has tendered his resignation, "ring, as be says, to the gravity of the Parliamentary situation. He says that a strong Cabinet is necessary, °wing to the complexity of European affairs. ST. div.head: IMPERIAL
div.p: IMPERIAL

HOUSE OF LORDS.—Moirnar.. The Lord Chancellor took his seat shortly after 4p The Blackburn Corporation Tramways Bill, the Lan- cashire County Justices Bill, and the Manchester Cor- poration Bill were read a second time. Lvxhcr.—ThO Lonn CRAiicarmon, in moving tho second reading of the Lunacy Acts Amendment Bill, pointed out that except in one respect it was substan- tially a measure to which their lordships had given their approval in, two successive sessions. He read a state- ment Trcm he Commissioners of Lunacy in which they urged the late Lord Shaftesbury's objections to a judi- cial examination of the patient before any person could be placed under restraint as a lunatic; but he said he regarded that point as one now beyond the range 1 t of controversy, because there was a very general feeling outside and a concurrence of opinion on both sides of t their lordships' House that in cases of alleged lunacy there was need of further protection for the liberty of the subject. Accordingly he had introduced in this bill a section providing that before any person could be placed under restraint on the ground of lunacy notice should be served on him to iriform him that he might apply to a magistrate for the holding of a judi- cial investigation to ascertain whether he ought to be deprived of his liberty.—Lord ilsescrnam, while giving a general approval to the bill, reserved his opinion on the new section as to judicial examina- tions.—Lord Mitvrowx quoted a written opinion ex- pressed by the late Lord Shaftesbury thatprivate lunatic asylums ought to be compulsorily abolished. The bill was then read a second time, as was also the Lunacy bill, the object of which the Lord Chancellor explained to be codification of the various statutes relating to lunacy. Lord Cnoss, in reply to 'Lord Stanley of Alderley, stated that he had advised her Majesty to accept the resignation of Mr. Sullivan, of the Covenanted Civil Ser- vice of India.

Lord HARRIS, in answer to Lord Erne, stated that the sword bayonets which were reported to have bent when in use on board one of her Majesty's ships were of a make in use from 1874 up to last year, and did not stand the present test, which was much more severe than the one applied in 1874. THE COURT OF APPEAL.—The LORD CHANCELLOR, in moving the second reading of the Appellate Jurisction Bill, explained that it would make three amendments in the Act of 1876. First, it would enable law lords who wished to assist in the hearing of appeals to take the oath when Parliament was not sitting; next, It would remove the disability of every law lord who had resigned the office of Lord of Appeal in Ordin- ary to receive a writ of summons entitling him to take part in the business of the House of Lords; and thirdly, it would enable the Crown to give the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council the assistance of persons who had held high legal positions in India. While referring to the second object of the bill, the noble and learned lord paid a high 'tribute to the services which Lord Blackburn had ren- dered to the jurisprudence of the country.—After a short conversation, in which Lords Fitzgerald, Herschel!, Milltown, and Denman took part, the bill was read a second time.
The Pluralities Act Amendment Bill passed through Committee.
Their Lordships rose at 5 50 p.m HOUSE OF COMMONS.—MONDAH:

The Speaker took the Chair at 4 p.m. Over Darwen Corporation Bill was read a second time. Mr. Banbury gave notice that he should take an early opportunity to call attention to the defective system of administration in the Ordnance Department, under which it was a common occurrence for bad and ineffi- cient weapons to be issued to her Majesty's naval and military forces. (Hear, hear.)

THE ADDRESS.—MR. PARNELL'S AMENDMENT. • The debate on the Address was resumed. Mr. Paaa-stt moved the following amendment : But humbly to represent to her Majesty that the relations between the owners and occupiers of land in Ireland has not seriously been disturbed in the cases of those owners who have granted to their tenants such abate- ments of rents as are called for by the state of prices of agricultural and pastoral products, and that the remedy for the existing crisis in Irish agrarian affairs is not to be found in increased stringerici- of criminal procedure, or the pursuit of such novel, doubtful, and unconstitutional measures as have recently been taken by her Majesty's Government in Ireland, but in such a reform of the law and the system of government as will -satisfy the needs and secure the confidence of the Irish people." He said it would firstly be his duty to attach serious blame to the Government for the rejection of the Tenants' Relief Bill of last session, which, in his opinion would have effectively prevented the very limited disturbLices—(lrish cheers)—secondly, to show that coercion would fail, as it always had failed, and would prevent the bringing about of a better state of things in Ireland, whether between owner or servant, or in what he might call the international relations between England and Ireland. (Ironical Ministerial and Opposition approving cheers.) If the Government understood the coercion they foreshadowed in the speech from the Throne—a coercion which was called by the euphonious name of 'alteration or reform in criminal procedure"— the result would be that the Chief Secretary would find himself at the top of an inclined plane, and that he would speedily, like Oliver Twist, be found in this House asking for " mdre." (Irish laughter and cheers.) The coercion the right hon. gentleman contemplated was coercion against his political friend in Ireland—the author of the plan of campaign—(Trish cheers),—who appeared to have entered into competition with the Government as to who, should produce the best plan for taking a short cut to the government of Ireland. (Irish cheers.) All reference in Ireland showed that when they stopped a political agita- tion, muzzled their political opponents and put them in gaol, they would only have to begin again, end that open speaking having been stopped and thrust underthe surface the Government would immediately find themselves face to face with the terrible secret societies, and with the revival of agrarian and political crime in its worst forms. He trusted that whilst there was yet time the right hon. gentleman and the Government might be dissuaded from entering upon this course and rely upon the removal of grievances, the amelioration of the law, and the altera- tion of the system of government in Ireland. (Irish cheers.) He also blamed the Government for appealing to the inherent jurisdiction of the Queen's Bench to de- prive the member for: East Mayo of his liberty and in proclaiming the Sligo meeting. Another example of meanness—he could not invent a less harsh term—was their transferring the trial from the city to the county of Dublin, where they thought they would get more sub- servient jurymen. (Irish cheers., If the Crown suc- ceeded in convicting his hon. friend by the adoiation of such a mean trick—(lrish cheers)—neither the justice of the verdict, tier the validity of the proceedings would be recognised by any Irish member worthy of the name. (Loud and prolonged Irish cheering.) He did not intend to condemn the Government for their dispensing action in Ireland, but at the same time he had to state that this dispensing action could not be held to, absolve the Government from the consequence of rejecting the Ten- ants' Relief Bill of last year, the rejection of which was the source and origin of every disturbance. (Ironical Ministerial and counter Irish cheers.) That bill Was thrown out, but would anybody contend that there was no necessity for a large and general reduction of rents? He would have the House to bear in mind that they were face to face with a Government bench which had no plan of reform for Ireland, no plan for the amelioration °Me condition of the tenant, no plan for easing the relations between landlord and tenant except the shifting, stumb- ling, broken-kneed processes—(lrish cheers)—carried out through the instrumentality of Judge Curran and General Buller. (Renewed Irish cheering.) He (Mr. Fermi)) undoubtedly did err on the side of modesty and moderation in making his Land Bill, which ' the House rejected, only applicable to judicial tenants; but that was not an argument against it which the Government could use. Referring to the Glenbeigh evictions, be said that the unusually large amount of arrears which was owing arose from the fact that the landlord and mortgagees were in contention, each claiming the rent, and in a " No-rent manifesto" asking the tenants to withhold it from the other; but for the harsh conduct of the land- lord, who first demanded full rent and costs, the matter would have been settled. The National League never interfered there at all until the evictions were in full • swing, but if the plan of campaign had been adopted, and the twenty-five solvent tenants had not paid until those who could not pay had had their rents reduced, he believed there would have been no evictions or house burning% (Opposition cheers.) The experience of history had shown Ireland that she had nothing to Q:aitt by respect of law and order, by depending upon constitutional methods, and by looking to Par- liament for the redress of their grievances. The present Government in rejecting his bill again taught the Irish people that bad old lesson. The vreatest secrecy had. been maintained with regard to the proceedings and sayings of General Buller, and whenever any'awkward fact came out it was stoutly denied until the proof was 'too strong. With regard to the plan of campaign, he could speak of it freely and fairly as one who was in no sense respoesible for it. (Home Rule cheers and ironical counter cheers.) He denied in the strongest terms that there was any foundation for the state- ment that the plan of campaign had disturbed the relation, between landlord and tenant, and he condemned in the strongest manner the action of the Government in not at once denouncing the plan if, as they now held, it was illegal. (Home Rule cheers.) The fact was, the Government -were trying to do the same thing as was being done by the hon. methher for East Mayo and Mr. W. O'Brien, and they were jealous because they did not succeed so well as those hon. members. (Rear, hear.) But those who acted for the plan of cam- paign did not act in the helter-skelter, slap-dash way in which General Buller and Judge Curran were acting. They made care{ ul inquiry into every case, and took up no case in which there was not immediate necessity for reduction. (Hear, hear.) Lord Salisbury had talked about robbery and embezzlement, but it was not wise to speak thus , in connection with the Irish land question. Those who did so forgot that almost every title to Irish land was founded on robbery and embezzleibent. (Loud Home ' Rule cheer...) His next proposition involved a condenana.- non of coercion as a remedy for troehlea in Ireland. He • would remind the House that the late Mr. Forattr corn-

div.head: PARLIAMENT.
div.p: PARLIAMENT.
THE EXAMINER, S A TURDAY, FEBRUARY 12. 1.887.

menced by only wanting an Act to put down the village tyrants and dissolute ruffians, but he ended with an Act more sweeping than anything that had ever been passed before. The (,N-imes Act was followed from Amenca by dynamite explosions which threatened the public build- ings of the country and caused loss of life, and even the Ministers of the day were not safe from violent attack, while the animosity between the two countries reached a height which it had not attained since 1798. (Hear, hear.) What was the result of all that? A Tory Government came into office and abandoned coercion—(cheers from the Home Rulers)—but there could be no betwixt and between in the matter of coercion. Although the right hon. gentleman might get his Coercion Act to put down political offenders, he would not be able to stop there. He would be eventually hurried on from one measure of repression to another, and he would not be able to stop until he had to make his choice between such measures of repression as the Czar of Russia would administer, but which the right hon. gentleman would never- be able to administer under the present Constitution and as long as they kept the Irish members in the Imperial Parliament. (Loud cheers.) If they stopped coercion and repression now they would succeed. Coercion had done more to demoralise the Trish peasantry than all the Irish agitators from New York to San Francisco. If the Government would be warned in time they would do that which was just and right. If they attended to the wants and wishes of the Irish people and allowed Ireland to be self-governed, the Irish would show by making their own laws, by their tranquillity and peaceful mien, how unfairly and libellously they had been treated. The hon. gentleman concluded by moving his amendment, after speaking an hour and a half. Mr. P. M'HoNeui seconded the amendment. Mr. BAGGALLAY denied that the Government had acted in an unconstitutional way in respect to the plan of compaign, and argued that the utterances of Nationalist members in regard to it had been not only novel and doubtful but immoral and criminal. _ .

. Mr. HAYDEN and Mr. BLADE spoke in support of the amendment: Mr. JOHNSTON dwelt upon the impartiality of Protestant juries and the determination of the Orange- men to rnalntain the Union; and Mr. Prmourrow, who repudiated the suggestion that the Catholics of Ireland desired revolution, maintained that landlordism had done more harm thaa all the secret societies.

Mr. Ilawarms remarked upon the ingenuity of the wording of the amendment, and argued that whatever alteration of the criminal law was proposed should be permanent He objected to Ireland being treated from a party point of view, and doubted whether the Orange members truly represented the Protestant feeling of that country. As to the land question, he urged that the Land Acts should be made to work more effectively, and evicted tenants ought to be secured their unexhauFted improvements. Labour and capital were both required in Ireland, and he was opposed to the emigration of the tenants or the extirpation of the landlords.

--- The ATIVINEY-GENIMAL for IRELAI,7I) dissented from every proposition in the amendment, and. denying Mr. Parnell's assertion that the rejection of his bill was at the root of all the mischief, he contended that all Mr. Parnell's predictions as to what was about to happen had failed, and that agitation was the cause of all the disturb- ances. As to the Glenbeigh evictions, Mr. Parnell's bill would not have met them, nor could they have been prevented by any agrarian legislation of any kind. Commenting on the plan of campaign, he described the intimidation by which it was en- forced, and pointed out, by numerous extracts from the speeches of Mr. O'Brien and others, that the intention of the Plan was to ruin the landlords and drive them out of the country. With regard to the dis- pensing power, he showed that not a scintilla of proof had been forthcoming of the charge against General Buller, Judge Curran, and others, and defended the legal proceedings at Sligo and Dublin. Mr. Dmr,ox referred to the packing of juries, and characterised the speech of the Attorney-General as an attempt to intimidate the jury by whom he would be tried next week. What brought the plan of campaign into operation, he said, was the discovery that a large number of landlords refused to be coerced by the Chief Secretary, and he maintained that the plan had prevented evictions on all those estates where it had been put into force. He further justified it by reference to the administration of justice in Irish County Courts, quoting numerous instances in which the law had been administered in compliance with the exigencies of the case, and not strictly in accordance with the rights of the parties. Referring to the decrease in the population of Ireland during the last 40 years, he main- tained that it was solely the result of evil laws and an evil system. Ile ridiculed the idea of removing the people without altering the system, and he warned the Government against is policy of migration which the people, he said, V. 3uld understand to mean a policy of extermination.
The debate was adjourned on the motion of Mr_ J. MORLEY. and after some further business the House ad- journed at 12 55 a.m.
HOUSE OF LORDS.-TLIESDAY.

The Lord Chancellor took his seat at 4115 p.m. The Bishops of Winchester, Chichester, Bath and Welts, and Hereford, and Lord Tollemache and the Earl of Courtown took the oath and subscribed the roll. The Pluralities Bill was read a third time and passed. THE SALE OF GLEBE LANDS. —Lord CROSS presented and asked their Lordships to give a first reading to a bill to facilitate the sale of glebe lands in England, and to take advantage of such sale for the purpose of providing a number of small allotments for persons suited for them. As to the first object, the bill was not compul- sory, but permissive. The bill proceeded upon the assumption that it was expedient that the country clergy should, if they wished, be relieved from the ownership of lands. There were now safer and more profitable investments open to the general public. He proposed that the Land Commissioners should be at liberty to carry out the sale on the application of the clergyman, after he had given notice to the patron and to the bishop, and the Commissioners were not to sanction the sale unless they were of opinion that it would be for the benefit not only of the incumbents but of the benefice. When the glebe had been sold the purchase money would be paid to the Land Commissioner, who would give a certificate securing to the purchaser an absolute and indefensible title, and the Commissioners would be entitled to invest the money in Government securities, or in the stock of such railway companies as, had for 10 years previously paid a certain dividend On their ordinary stock. The investment would be in the name of the bishop, the patron, and the incumbent, and the Land Commissioners would have power to retain a sufficient sum to put the property in proper repair. As to the second part of the bill it was proposed that till a county authority had been set up the Sanitary Authority should have power to purchase a portion of the pro- perty or the purpose of offering it in small allotments, and-to that end they would ho authorised to borrow money.—Earl GRANVILLE welcomed the noble lord in that House, but pointed out to him t, at it, was not the practice there to make without•notice a statement of the provisions of a bill on its introduction.—The Marqui, of SALISBURY agreed that notice ought to have been given, and accepted the responsibility for having misled the infant peer in the matter. (laughter.)—The bill was read a first time. Their lordships rose ax 5 0 p.n.
lIOtTSE OF COMMONS.-TSIESDAY.

THE COST OF THE ,GLENBEIGH EVICTIONS.—In reply to Mr. Conybeare, Sir. M. H. Beach said that the total cost to the British taxpayers oc the police employed in the Glenbeigh evictions was £451.—1n answer to a number of other questions, he said the sheriff had police protec- tion, as had Mr. Roe, and the police had done their duty iniprotecting the latter. MUZZLING OF Doos.—ln reply to Mr. H. S. Wright, Lord John MeNtatas said that local authorities through- out the country had already full powers to make compul- sory reiulations for the muzzling of dogs in their districts whenever, they thought necessary. It was, therefore, not the intention of the Government to take any further steps to compel the general muzzling of dogs all over the country.

THE DEBATE ON ,11111. • PARNELL'S AMENDMENT. The debate on Mr. Parnell's amendment to the address wiis resumed by Mr. hto. MORLEY, who said that the amendment pointed to future policy as well as to past administration, and his desire was' to ascertain how far the past shed a light on our future policy. Per his part he should have no hesitation in going into the lobby with the hon. member for Cork. There was, he said, no remedy for the existing crisis that was not connected with such a reform as would win the confidence ot the Irish people. Had anything happened under the ad- ministration of the present Government to warrant our confidence being reposed in the Government ? They bad heard much about what would be the result of a firm Government, but the fact was that there had been no abatement of the position in Ireland during the existence of the present Administration. . It was very well now for the Government to talk about law and order, but there was no evidence of any strengthening of ' confidence in their rule, even among their own friends, to say nothing of their opponents. The conclusion to be 'drawn from all that had happened was that there was in Ireland a real wrong and a real danger. If it were said that the bill of Mr. Parnell last September was not the kind of remedy for this, why had not those who thought so shown the House what was the real remedy to apply? It must have been seen from the past history of Ireland that where there was a real grievance without a remedy it must necessarily be anticipated that illegal, and perhaps criminal, methods of re&ess would be resorted to. (Hear, hear.) He would not consent to argue the con- dition of Ireland on narrow technical grounds. It was, he said, admitted that anarchy did not prevail in Ireland, and Lord Hartington who had recently made this admis- sion, must see how it conflicted with his former assertion that the plan of campaign was subversive of the rules of social order. Whatever might be said of the plan of campaign it was at any rate better than the secret organisation which had been known to Ireland in former years. (Hear, hear.) Moreover, the plan of cam- paign was by . no means worse than the action Of those landlords m Ireland who, according to the present Chief Secretary, had behaved with great harshness as owners of property, without fulfilling the duties attach- ing to their position. (Cheers.) The Liberal party had been unfairly taxed with supporting everything pro- pounded by the Irish party becaustt'they concurred with 4

the Irish representatives in one proposition. This doe- trine he distinctly repudiated, and retorted on the Con- servaive party themselves. The Liberals were under no obligation to support everything that was proposed by the Irish members, but they were not to be driven by taunts of this sort from supporting that which they held to be right and expedient. The right hon. gentleman here referred to the action taken by the present Govern- ment in the removal of Sir Robert Hamilton, which must have had a prejudicial effect on the prospects of the prewnt Government in the good government of Ireland, especially in its tendency to prevent experienced officials from tendering to the Irish Executive sound advice, which they thought might not prove accept- able. (Hear, hear.) It was, lie said, stated that changes were about to be made which would end in the office of Under-Secretary being made a political office, the result,of which would inevitably be to throw any power the office might possess into the hands of the lawyers. Such a state of things would certainly be highly distasteful to the Irish people. (Hear, hear.) Turning to ahother matter, the right hon. gentleman cited the exclusion of Catholics from the Sligo juries, and called attention to the avowal made last night that that was not the result of acci- dent, but of design. There could be no doubt that the rule that jurors should be indifferently chosen had been broken, and the excuse was that the Crown wanted to secure men of independent thought, this Wear a euphemism for men who would be sure to convict (Hear, hear.) Was it, he asked, surprising that, with maxims and actions like these, her Majesty's Government could not govern Ireland? He (Mr. Morley) supported the amendment of Mr. Parnell, because he held that it indi- cated the only policy that could be adopted in regard to Ire- land. They had hoard a good deal about emigration, which had been recommended by Lord Hartington as a thing to be carried out by the Government But surely this was not a policy to be undertaken without reference to the feelings of the Irish people, and he put it to the House what would be the effect of sending abroad to any of the colonies batches of poor, distressed, and broken- down creatures, such as had been the subject of the recent evictions. (Hear, hear.) As to the establishment of a Board of Emigration under the control of the Government, Mr. Luke had reported, in 1884, that such was the state of things in Ireland at that time that the establishment of such a board was impossible, and he (Mr. Morley) put it to the House whether, if such a thing was impossible in 1884, it was at all feasible in the state of things existing in 1887. (Hear, hear.) The right hon. gentlemen went on to review the course of recent legislation in regard to Irish land, pointing out that, notwithstanding the favour- able nature of that legislation, the Irish tenants had shown no eager desire to avail themselves of the advan- tages thus conceded. That being so, it seemed to follow that it was not in that direction that they must look for the full remedy they desired to obtain for the present state of things. Replying to the speech made on the previous night by Mr. Wodehouse, the right hon. gentleman asked whether it was supposed that the exigencies of political parties were about to be terminated? Was it possible, in the face of the experience of late years, to expect that such exigencies were to come to an end, and they were to go on in future with a single and permanent policy for Ireland? It was not, furthermore, in the direction of coercion that any remedy was to be anticipated for the stateof things existing in Ireland. Lord R. Churchill had lately said Home Rule was now at an end, but the noble lord was not a trustworthy prophet in regard to Ireland. He had, for instance, prophesied that the exten- sion of the franchise in Ireland would result in the swamp- ing by the Irish counties of the Nationalistic party. They had heard much of the need of local government for Ireland, but there was little prospect of this being achieved under the programme submitted by the Go- vernment. Was there over, he asked, a session begun with so little prospect of necessary legislation? Was there ever a session opened in so leaden an atmosphere? (Ministerial cheers.) The Government cheered that re- mark, but he asked—Whose fault was it? (Opposition cheers.) It was his firm conviction that the leaden cloud he had referred to would not lift from the delibera- tions of the House until they had achieved such a reform in the system of government in Ireland as would meet the needs of the Irish people. (Cheers.) It was because he, held this conviction that he should vote for the amend- ment of the hon. member for Cork. (Cheers.) Mr. Howoaru following, taunted the Opposition on the absence of their leader, and advocated a scheme of emigra- tion for settling the Irish difficulty.—Sir E. GREY, as a young member, addressing the Hones for the firest time, , made a very favourable impression, and did justice to his antecedents, by the clear manner in which he worked out an argument that the true policy in Ireland was to place upon the people of Ireland the responsibility for their own good government —Debate went on for a time in the bands of Colonel Waring, Mr. E. Robertson, Mr. H Wright, Mr. E. Harrington, and other members.—On the motion of Mr. B. COLERIDGE, the debate was adjourned. GLkER LANDS.—Mr. BAGGALLAY obtained leave to bring in a bill to amend the law relating to the occupation of glebe lands by incumbents in England. The House adjourned at twenty minutes to one. HOUSE OF COMMONS..--WEDNESDAY.

The Speaker took the chair at twenty minutes after' twelve o'clock. PE:lTlONS.—Petitions were presented in favour of Sun- day closing by Mr. W. H. Houldsworth from the Women's Christian Temperance Association, Manchester ; and by Mr. Edwards• Moss, from Widnes, for the consideration of the case of William Buchanan. THE DEBATE ON TEE ADDRESS;--The debate OR Mr Parnell's amendment to the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne was resumed.—Lord ERRINGTON said be could not see where the Plan of Campaign differed from the "No Rent" manifesto which was suppressed by Mr. Wad- stone's Government —Mr. T. GILL denounced the recent action of the Irish Queen's Bench in the case of Mr. Dillon, which, he said, war without precedent since the days of the Star Chamber.—Mr. W. Long condemned the Plan of Cam- paign, and remarked that though he had no sympathy with bad landlords, he was far from saying that the Government oupt not to extend to them that protection of the law which was every man's priyilege.—Mr. B. COLERIDGE be- lieved that the Plan of Campaign bad commended itself to the moral sense of the majority of the English people.— Mr. W. R. M'Laren held that at the worst Vac Plan of Campaign was only a technical violation of tho doubtful law of conspiracy, and' he would not censure Irish members for having put it into operation. He helieved if the Government would pass such a measure of Home Rule as was foreshadowed in the amendment it would solve the Irish difficulty.—The Sorterron GENERAL (Sir E. Clarke) declared that the plan of campaign was undoubtedly an legal conspiracy between tenants who could pay their rents illegal tenants who could not to coerce the landlords into abandoning to some extent their legal rights as against all Of them, whether they could pay or whether they could not. The House might, he said, take his word for it that there was no foundation for the prophecy that they would soon be called upon to consider a bill for patting Irish mem- bers into prison. He believed that the object of the present attack was to defeat the efforts of the Government to corn- ' pose the dieorders in Ireland.—Mr. SYDNEY BUXTON con- tended that such a scheme of emigration as had been pro- posed could only be carried out by the agency of an Irish Parliament—The debate was adjourned on the motion of Mr. W. REDMOND.

The test was applied on four vessels, and most of the sword-bayonets and cutlasses were found to be defec- tive. On the Devastation many of the sword-bayonets bent like hoop-iron, and some could be easily bent by the band and remained bent.—Mr. STANHOPE proposed to institute an independent inquiry into the cbndition of the weapons now complained of, and he should ask the First Lord of the Admiralty to nominate a representative to take part in it.

ent to what obtained in this country. He thought the Government took a right course in prosecuting those who were the authors of the Plan rather than the tenants who were the instruments by which it was put into execution. If the Plan of Campaign could not be suppressed, if it could not be stopped, there was an end of all legal rela- Voris between tenant and landlord ; and if the policy was persevered with the only remedy left in the landlord's hands was not partial but indiscriminate and total eviction if be wished to retain his title. It was the duty of the Govern- ment to do everything in their power to prevent the further progress of a system which could only lead to such results. He declined to vote for a resolution which held up that the only object was to satisfy the wants and to secure the con- fidence of the Irish people, and which failed to recog- nise that these were securities which were equally re- quired for the people of Great Britain before they could give assent to any such measure as that now proposed. SHOCKING INHIIMANITE.—At Leeds Assizes, on Thursday, an elderly man named liaadfiergh, living at Todroorden, was convicted of baying deprived his wife of food, with intent to murder her. The woman, who suffered from paralysis, was left by the prisoner for days together, lying helpless on a filthy mattress and dependent on the charity of neighbours for food. Mr:Justice Day passed the utmost sentence the law allowed—two years' imprisonment. GREAT FIRE IN DroolAN —On Thursday morning the Four Courts were discovered to be on fire. The whole pile of bttildings were enveloped in smoke, and flames were la- suing from the windows. The Vice-Chancellor's Court, in I the west wing, was entirely gutted, and the books and fur- niture destroyed. After two hours' exertion the fire was subdued, and preyented extending to the rest of the splendid pile of buildings. The fire originated in the passage to the Vice-Chancellor's Court. The cause is unascer- tained. GHLORO.LINSEED Conon LOZENGES a medicated Ilreeed extract, 6d; postage 2d. fey. Bros.. Stockuort, and all Chemists.—A Vt. THE REGULATION OF MINES.—A deoutation representing miners in all parts of the United kingdom waited on Thursday upon the Home Secretory to urge the embodi- ment of certain suggestions in the new Mines Regulation Bill of the Government. The depu lotion desired to have the employment of women about collieries prohibited, after a time, if not forthwith. They also asked for the appoint- ment of additional inspectors, and an improvement in the method of inspection, for the .more stringent testing of lamps, the fixing of responsibility on some offi- cial in case of accident, and the appointment of a Minister of Mines. Mr. Matthews. in reply, said he hod already carefully corsiderrd the points raised As to female employment, he would like to hear what the women thought. If, as the deputation said, the work, though hard, did not deteriorate the women's morals ner injuriously affect their health, the matter should be left for the women themselves to decide, and it was a little harsh .for 'nen to say that women and gir s should be shut oat of their labour. The Home Secretary promised to submit his bill, before presenting it to Parlia nenr, to gentlemen re- presenting both miners and owners, for their suggestions. Dre,amakers can buy no better sewing cotton than Bagley and Wright's, which for strength is unequalled.-4dvt.

div.head: ADDRESS.
div.p: THE ADDRESS.

Mr. W. REDMOND resumed the debate en the Address in reply to the Speech from the Throne. Blaming the Govern- ment for delaying, during two months, to declare the Plan of Campaign illegal, be said the Irish people were ready to meet tbe people of this country half way in establishing a firm system of land tenure and of legislative indepen- dence.

Lord HABTINGTON wished to recall the attention of the House to the real nature of the amendment. He believed that perfectly satisfactory relations would never be estab- lished in Ireland except by some process which would do away with the dual ownership which had been created, and which would to a large extent make the occupier of the land of Ireland the proprietor of the land. But that ques- tion coul I not be settled in a discussion on an amendment of the character before the House, and could only be ap- proached on deliberate and definite proposals placed before the House by a responsible Government. It was, he con- tended, no remedy for the existing state of things to suspend or reduce, r even abolish, the payment of rent. The only remedy was the increase of productive employment in Ire• land, or some means of escape from the place where the people could not be productively employed. He did not believe in compulsory emigration, but he did in volun- tary emigration. Referring to the alleged jury packing, the right bon. Marquis said he did. not think there were grounds for the allegation, though I no doubt there were proceedings resorted to in Ireland differ-

div.p: POLICE INTELLIGENCE.
WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. SATURDAY—Before Alderman Bargees and Alderman
Chandlev.

A SERVANT OF THE QllREN.—Michad Callighan (20), a rough looking young fellow, who boasts that he never works except for the Queen, was charged with being drunk and disorderly in Union-street on Friday afternoon, and also with assaulting Constables Baxendale and Corcoran, and damaging the uniform of another corstable. When seen to be drunk he was requested to go quietly home, but refused and was taken into custody. He then became violent, kicked the officers, butted them in the stomach, and other- wise ill-treated them. He remarked that when released he would "do" ten years for one of the constables, and made use of other violent threats as he was being taken to the station. It was his twentieth appearance: For the drun- kenness he was sent to prison for a month, and for assault- ing the policemen he was committed to prison for six months.

MONDAY—Before Alderman Harrison (deputy Mayor), and Councillors Greening and Francomb. MTSCELLANEOI7B.—Tbe following persons were fined for drunkenness: David Knowles, John Locker, Caleb Skid- more, and Michael Smith, and Jane Shepherd and Joseph Miller, who were charged with begging, were dismissed with a caution.—Two young men named Harris and Hunt were bound over in their own recoguisances to keep the peace on a charge of fighting in the Market-place.—Walter Cotton and David Broderick were summoned for ill-treating a horse by driving it at a quick speed when it was drawing a load of a ton of coals, on the 31st January. They said that the horse only willoped about twenty yards. Fined 5s and costa—Wiliam Fitzpatrick and Thomas Williams were each fined 5s and costa for driving furiously in Knatsford- road on the 28th ult., and Martin Mannion was fined 5s and costs for furiously driving in Horsemar- ket-street.—James Griffin, William Edelsten, and Thomas Stockton, for playing ate hinty in Buckley-etreet,were each fined 2s 6d, including costs, I Daniel Atherton and Mark Ryder, charged with shooting missiles faom a catapult, were each fined Is, including costs.—James Rimmer was fined Is for allowing the chimney of his dwelling-house to be on fire.

FolooL ArrEmomicE.—Mr. George Riley prosecuted the following persons for neglecting to send their children to echool : Thomas Taylor, William Farrington, John Win. nett, John Harper. Edward Murray, John Henry Gorton, George Harper, William Jones, and Hannah Ward. BREACH OF THE PEtiCK —Albert Young and John Brown, joiners, were charged with fighting in Church-street. Farn- worth, and were each bound over to be of good behaviour for two months.

Millington, Woodward was bound over M keep the peace. Kennedy did not appear. CHIMNEY ON FlRE.—Elizabeth Whitby, of Percival'e- lane, was fined 6d, and costs 98 63, for allowing the chimney of her dwelling-house to 3e on fire. Breeze, was fined 108 and costs for being drunk and dis- orderly at Clifton, en Saturday night. "NOT QUITE Rictwr."—Randell Bennett, an elderly man, was charged with having at halt-ptst four o'clock on Sun- day morning, stolen a hundredweight of coal, worth Bd, belonging to the Weaver Navigation Company. P.C. Dale deposed to seeing the prisoner come to a coal heap along , the canal side at Weston Point. and partially fill a large bag. The prisons: contended that the captain of a steam boat had given him the coal. His wife informed the magi- strides that the prisoner was not accountable for Ms actions, and Superintendent Hollingwortb was of the same opinion. He bad, however, offended so often in this manner that Captain Clark felt compelled to take action. Mr. Reynolds said the prisoner was evidently not in his right mind, and suggested that he should go to the Workhouse. Prisoner: I'm not going to the Workhouse. (Laughter.) Eventually be was discharged with a caution.

div.head: GENERAL NEWS.
div.p: GENERAL NEWS.
The Shrewsbury Corporation, on Mottday, resolved unanimously to petition against the Liverpool Water Bill.

It is asserted that Sir Evelyn Wood's committee have practically decided to adopt the Lee American repeating rifle. At Sheffield, on Monday, a coal dealer, named Ilibbert, was killed by his horse running away and throwing him headlong on the kerbstone. The Lord Chief Justice, referring, on Monday, to the business of the courts, said the Crown list of cases was the heaviest in his experience—as many as 226 eases.
Lord Mostyn has intimated his intention of presenting the Happy Valley, Llandudno, to the town as a publio pleasure ground, in commemoration of the Queen's Jubilee. _ _ _

_ At the Duke of Westminster's private chapel at Eaton Hall, Cheshire, on Monday, Countess Grosvenor was married, by special license, to Mr. G. Percy Wyndham. The honeymoon will be spent at Holkyn Castle. A coffin, containing the corpse of a young lady, named Marchaux, which went down in the steam packet Brighton, off the Guernsey coast, was landed at Guern- sey on Monday, having been picked up off Alderney on Saturday. It was intact, and was forwarded to Jersey for interment. •

Mr. Justice Chitty on Saturday decided an interesting point on the law that enables a young lady of seventeen to execute a valid settlement on her marriage. In the case in question the young lady had married under that age, but was now over it, and the judge sanctioned a post-nuptial settlement of her property. A deputation of miners waited on the Mayor of New- castle on Saturday with reference to the scheme of emigration to 'Western Australia. The Mayor replied that the time was not yet ripe for selecting emi- grants, as the funds were not yet available. In reply to the Mayor, the deputation stated that a number of men would prefer to emigrate irrespective of any improve- meat in the trade of the district. Five men, named Robert Grieve, Thomas Morgan, Duncan Mackenzie, James Milligan, and Peter Anderson, were seriously injured on Monday by an explosion of dynamite at the new harbour at Eyemouth, Berwick- shire. It appears that while they, with other labourers, were engaged in blasting operations, Grieve tried to force a dynamite cartridge into the piping by beating it with a stone. An explosion followed, with the result stated. Grieve was so seriously injured that his recovery is doubtful.

Excitement was caused in the Cqunty Magistrates' Court, Liverpool, on Monday, by a singular accident. Ora) of the prisoners awaiting trial was standing in the dock at the head of the stairs leading to the cells. The stairs are stone, and very steep. The prisoner by some mean& slipped, and fell from the top to the bottom, striking his head so severely that when picked up he was uncoil- scious. Medical aid was summoned and everything done to restore consciousness, but without avail, and the man was removed to the infirmary, where he died.

ANTI-VACCINATORS SI7PPORTRD sv OTIARDIANS.—Th Local Government Board have again called the attention of the Leicester Guardians to the extraordinary position of the town as regards vaccination, and the new pro- secutions of defaulters just issued, show that, of 7,200 births, only 1,609 were vaccinated, and none of the 6,600 new defaulters were prosecuted. The Guardians resolved to take no action, leaving the inhabitants free choice.

AN OLDHAM MYSTERY.—On Sunday morning,upon the ostler at the Bull's Head, Oldham, going into the stable he was horrified to find a man named Isaac Hall, resid- ing at 4, Cross-street, lying on the floor dead and quite cold. Hall had been drinking in the Bull's Head on Saturday afternoon, and must have gone into the stable to get a rest. He appears to have been going into tho loft or coming from it, as he was found lying at the foot of the ladder, and on examination his neck was found to be broken. •

„—... COTTAGZ Bantu:sm.—Mr. Agg-Gardener, 'chairman of the County Brews' Society, has issued a circular to members of Parliament calling attention to the recent abolition of the license for cottage brewing for houses under the annual value of £B, by which all persons living in houses under that value are enabled to brew beer for their own consumption free of duty and without any supervision. They suggest the advisability of requiring' all persons who brew beer without a license to register their names once a year, so that it may be known who is going to brew during the ensuing year.

THE Davossmint MYSTERY.—An adjourned inquiry into the circumstances attending the death of Selina Lever, houskeeper to the vicar of Stoke Gabriel, Devon, took place on Monday. The county analyst sent in a re- port in which he stated that he could find no trace of poison, and it was alc° stated that the medicine pro- vided by a "medical scientist" was harmless. The jury, after deliberating for an hour and a quarter, returned a verdict of 0 Death from natual• causes," adding a rider to the effect that the vicar was greatly to blame for not calling in medical assistance, and censuring the nurses for not suggesting such a course to him.

Lamb, 48, sboemaketo. charged 'with attempting to murder his sister:in4BW was sentenced to fifteen years' penal servitude. Simeon Holt, a tradesmen, aged 65, hanged himself ba; a police cell on Saturday at Bolton, whilst awaiting: examination on a charge of criminally assaulting a At Wolverhampton Police Court, on Monday, a llcensek victualler, named Thomas Cox Hartshorne, was fin* £lO and costs for permitting card-playing in-his house,l and attempting to bribe a policeman. - •

sharebroker of Sheffield named Armstead recently, left, the town and was declared bankrupt. The creditors+ met on Monday, and the official receiver informed them that Armstead's liabilities exceeded £12,000, and that the, assets were just over £.300.

At Bow-street Police-court, on Saturday, Heinrich Felbermann and Charles Wilkinson, the proprietor and publisher of Life, were committed for trial on a charge of Inving libelled Dr. Thomas Bird, one of the co-respon- dents in the Campbell Divorce case. A CHILD'S BODY FOUND IN A DITCIL—The body of a! male child, about two months old, has been discovered. in a ditch at Bishpool, about four miles from Newport (Mon.)' It was dressed in long clothes. Near it was g& feeding bottle and tube. A post-mortem examination, has been ordered. _ . _ _

Mr. H. M. Stanley embarked at Suez on Sunday after-4 , noon on board the British India Co.'s steamer Navarino,; bound direct for Zanzibar. lie is accompanied by Dr., ' Parke, of the Army Medical Department, and 61 trainedl black soldiers who have volunteered from the Egyptian, army. Sir William Harcourt gave a dinner party at Grafton- street on Saturday evening. The guests were Lady' Randolph Churchill, Mr. John Morley, the Bishop of New' York, the Hon. C. R. Spencer, Mr. and Lady Fanny! Majoribanks, the Marquis and Marchioness of Carmar-1 then, Lady Airlie, Mr. and Mrs. Oppenheim, and Lord, and Lady Howe. An influential meeting on Monday of the Glasgow! Merchants' House unanimously agreed tO ask the Govern-, ment to erect the Glasgow Royal Infirmary Medical; School into a college of Glasgow University. The Lord! Dean said the stueents of the school were tea few for the infirmary, the cause being the great distance from the. university. At a Council meeting of the Balloon Society of Great' Britain, in London, on Saturday. a letter was read from— Lord R. Churchill, acknowledging a resolution pro-, testing against the enormous increase in the standing. armies of Europe, and adding he questioned the wisdom of the principle that peace is best preserved by pre-. paring for war. It has been felt that. it would be gratifying to the nation if effect were given to a wish which has been, generally and widely expressed by the friends of the late Earl of Iddesleigh that some public memorial should be raised in his honour. A scheme has accordingly been set on foot with this object, and a general committee; composed of leading members of both political parties, will meet shortly in order to decide what form the memorial shall taka, and to make the necessary arrange- ments for the collection of funds.

The minority supporting Mr. Cremer's amendment to. the Address on the Egyptian question was composed of 54 Gladstonian Liberals, including Mr. Shaw Lefevre, four Unionist Liberals tMe.ssrs. Caine, It Chamberlain. Kenrick, and T. It Russell), and 41 Nationalists. The majority was made up of 228 Conservatives, 24 Unionist Liberals (including Lord Hartington, Mr. Seßar, Mr. Finlay, Mr. Sinclair, and Sir Donald Currie), and 13 Gladstonian Liberals (including Mr. Campbell-Banner- man, Mr. Marjoribanks, and Mr. Woodall).

THE SALFORD CORPORATION SCANDAL.—WIGAN GAS MANAGER DISMISSED.—On Monday, a meeting of the Wigan Gas Committee dealt with the connection of their gas engineer, Mr. Hawkins, with the above case tnd it was resolved to immediately suspend him. A letter had been received from him tendering his resignation. It was resolved, at a meeting of Altrincham tradesmen yesterday, to draw up an illuminated address for presen- tation to Mr. Lever, thanking him for the public service he has rendered in exposing corruption at the Salford Gasworks. _ _ _

DF.ATH OF DR. Joint Wszers.—Dr. John Watts, who had taken a prominent part in all educational, and many social movements for the benefit of the working classes for the last half century, (lied on Monday, at Man- chester, after a lingering illness, which for a long time had compelled him to abstain froni all active work. Dr. Watts was an active worker in the Anti-Corn Law agitation, and a member of the Cotton Famine Relief Committee, and afterwards wrote an exhaustive "His- tory of the Cotton Famine." He was one of the leading advocates of the Public Schools Association, and was the right hand man of Mr. Milner Gibson in the agitation for the removal of the taxes on knowledge. Utinenanotistn Wuur.s. A correspondent having written to the Right Hon. H. C. Raikes, Postmaster- General, with reference to the breakdown of telegraph wires during the recent snowstorms, has received the following reply :—" General Postoffice, London, Feb. 3, 1887. Sir,—ln reply to that portion of your letter of the 28th nit:, in which you ask whether certain recent state- ments to the effect that arrangements are being made to lay undereround the wires yip a large scale are correct, I am directed by the Postmaster-General to inform you that the question of connectin4 some of the chief towns- in the United Kingdom by underground lines of tele- graphs is now being considered by this department, but that no decision has yet been arrived at.—l am, sir, your obedient servant, Joni? ARDR/C"

WIFE MURDER THROUGH 7SALOVSY.—At the Notts Assizes, on Saturday, before Justice Field, Benjardin Terry, collier, was charged with the wilful murder of his wife, Mary Terry, at Old Basford, on Dezember 28th. The prisoner believed that his wife had been unfaithful to him, and made up his mind to murder her. He took a poker upstairs, but having had a shilling's worth of gin fell asleep. In the early morning he struck her over the head with the poker. In the struggle she got on the bedroom floor, but he knelt on her chest and strangled her. Ile then informed some neighbours of what he had done, and gave himself up to the police. A doctor was at once summoned, but life was found to be quite extinct. The prisoner's suspicions as to his wife's infidelity proved to be false. The judge held that there was no justification, and the prisoner being found guilty be was sentenced to death. FIFTY-THREE THOUSAND POUNDS OF PUBLIC MONET SPENT ON A REPORT.—ThO Eirmiaghant Mail presents its readers with an illustration which, though the matter be a comparatively small one, throws some light on the recklessness with which the taFpayers' money is squan- dered. In the annual report ofithe Government Station- ery Office just published, some particulars are given of the printing of the report of the Challenger expedition. This voluminous publication may interest a few scienti- fic people, but what do our economical readers think it , has cost the public? Mind, this is only the bill for print- ing and publishing—the expense of the expedition itself...• is another matter altogether. Well, up to the present, 1 the net cost of the publication has reached about £53 000. and, as seven more quarto volumes have yet to be brought out before the work is finished, this one book will M all probability cost as much as the Birmingham Assize Courts. This is simply a waste of public money, and the man who steps in and unmasks such extravag- ance deserves well of the struggling taxpayers. .

ATM= TO MURDER A. POLICEITAN.—At Oldham, on Saturday .night, a youth named Alfred William Turner fired a pistol at Constable Howton and a man named. • Goodger. Some of the pellets entered the constable's back, bringing him on his knees, and Goodger was struck on the left temple by a pellet, and fell to the ground. Turner was arrested, and when charged said it was all a mistake, as he thought he had shot at another constable who had locked him np.—On Monday, Alfred .William Turner, news lad, sixteen years ot age, was charged; with shooting Constable Howton, with intent to kill, and also with shooting and wounding Andrew ' Gooder.—Howton gave evidence, and said that there were five wounds in his back.—The man Gooder spoke to being shot on the temp/e.—Police-consta. ble Roach said he seized the prisoner immediately after he fired, and took a one-barrelled pistol from him. —Constable Bottomley said be bad of ten bien threatened by the prisoner for having taken him before the Watch Committee.—The Bench refused to reduce the charge to, one of aggravated assault, and committed the prisoner to the Assizes. MURDER IN MANCUESTER.—ARREST OF •A SUMTER. —A shocking murder was committed shortly after eleven o'clock on Saturday night, in the neighbourhood of , Ancoats. A number of roughs had been drinking at. various public-houses during the evening, and after' dosing time a serious quarrel arose in regard to some young women. The principals seem to have been Chas. Burns, a soldier in the 63rd (Mattche,ster) Regiment, stationed at Ashton-under-Lyne, and John Brady ,a dyer, , about 20 years of age, who lived in Back liolgate-street: It is stated that as Brady was walking home with two. girls Burns struck him in the face. The supporters of: Burns urged on a fight, and every effort was made by taunt and abuse to induce Brady to settle the dispute in; that summary manner. Brady, however, more discreet ; than valorous, walked away, and entered his house. The: others followed him to the door, and challenged him to come out and fight. He refused to do so, but appeared, on the doorstep, and commenced arguing again. From words he and the gang of roughs got to blows, and in, the scuffle he was stabbed several times in the breast- and abdomen. Be immediately cried " Um stabbed," and the party made off. Several of the crowd went to his assistance, and whilst two or three removed him into his houses young woman named Mary Ann Judge, a factory hand living at 23, Back Holgate-streeksrave information to Police-constable Firth, whom she found in Oldhatn-road. The officer immediately went to the house and found Brady lying on the floor bleeding profusely from a wound on the breast. Having obtained the assistance of another constable he procured a litter from Gonlden- street Police Station and conveyed the injured man to. the infirmary, but on arrival there life was found to be , extinct. From the information he got in the house the- other officer arrested the soldier Burns and took him to the station, where he was chargedwith having murdered Brady by stabbing him. It is expected that other. arrests will be made, and that two or three will ):+1 charged with the murdey - .

M !licocet.Tn ePARNELLts speech in the House of • --nloos, on Monday night, was a powerful nt of the policy of the Government. I._ here is no gainsaying his amendment to the fkddress. Sating it in simple terms, it sets fort that there have been no serious distur- Dances in Ireland where fair rents were de- banded; and that the remedy for the present c!isis is not to be found in repressive legisla- tl", " but in such a reform of the law and the sYstem of government as will satisfy the needs and secure the confidence of the Irish People." Mr. PARNELL threw upon the pre- ,iBe.ut Government the responsibility for such disturbance as has recently taken place; it was the inevitable outcome of their rejection .11,g the Tenants' Relief Bill of last session. -8 e Government as to this great blunder itdaud self-condemned. They scouted the _ea that th re was any need of the measure, and then when they were confronted by Wholesale writs of eviction served upon !...erlauts who were being called upon to pay laatuPossibi.e rents, they "exercised pressure," 1, the IRISH SECRETARY admitted, upon Irish t•Odlerds. How came they to do such a !ua, unless they found that they had been in the wrong in their supposition that Athere was no need for a Tenants' Relief Bill? o„nd if they were wrong, was this the right tO.rse to take to repair the error? Was it not atetLr duty rather to confess their fault, and seek, taitue earliest opportunity, to remedy the mis- Insetntb,eY had made by legislative enactment? to os,;au, however, of doing that they proceeded whro'°seeute Irish members of Parliament, task-- Were engaged, in another way, upon the ted 4,t0 'which the Goyetriment had commit- aernselyes, namely, putting pressure on Irish landlords Granted that the Plan of rhaulpaign might be open to question, was trir own conduct not questionable ? They or come into office as the special protectors Irish landlords ; they had pledged them- Ives up to the hilt to carry out the law= thutlgh it was their duty to do that whether the)! were pledged or not—vet the moment otieY were brought face to face with writs of thect,ion they turned tail, and began, outside looLaw, to " exercise pressure' on the land- -5 '4. If the Liberals, when in power,had done , sou)? such thing—if Mr. JOHN MORLEY had ' to exercise similar pressure—he would beencoon denounced from one end of the to'or:tY to the other as a traitor who declined ors-e'r°ree the law. But a Tory may steal a i.,,uetlarthile a Liberal must not look over the .;?rover' After coercing the landlords, the Irish raerit has proceeded to coerce the heck eaders ; the Plan of Campaign has been ,sl)TooounCed illegal ; meetings have the c Proclaimed ; and to attain their ends, teSort r"/ 11 authorities "have not hesitated to cnod t‘e t° jury packing. Mr. PARNELL re- Were o the case of Sligo, where three juries Offen constituted for the trial of agrarian Nlowe,,e,s, on which not a single Catholic was , Jury h'-'4 to sit, notwithstanding that in the ' konevAatiel "more than half the persons sum- ,,`"(ha-r— as jurors were Roman Catholics." ess th 'airn- Cart be more revolting to all ideas of d h., an a case like this? It is --mock ,qteu„, erY to ask Irishmen, under such itt4tic'ustances to respect the administration of 414 t e' just men are justified in despising thiz ,which is despicable. But having gone ther'ength, the Government would go fur- fur 12,hey are about to apply to Parliament 41'40 ,:tner powers of repression. They came coeki'ffice in the first instance as a party that the, and would govern without coercion ; thocabandoned the Crimes Act in order to 'l3'w mild they meant to be; but they !ere-tliv,Ut Passed through a single winter be- tZeY have to confess that they are power- tent " deal with the causes of Irish discon- Coer • „ overt, cion is to be the weapon of the iry of Toent that came into office with the ,rish No coercion " ; their remedy for "larq Isoontent is to make the Irish people t4ty- isco ritented. Happily the Liberal ve found out a new and a better trtiu before long the opportunity will, eat tr',...be given them to try the experi- tiorne Rule. Coercion has Idled Nrtld again • it will fail if continued, flowy D, I„ut n rase, for twenty years. What 4Cler.'e,cluired is; in the words of the Irish jstetil such, a 'reform of the land and the 'lueds a'c'f government as will satisfy the ' PeoPle.,;ld secure' the confidence of the Irish

oortan; a common observation that all im- throul:hrlltlventents for thF: public good pass itkcliff" three stages ; the first is the stage of rict thrence, the second that of Opposition, kence third that of triumph. The move- 'What nlakino. the Warrington Library thAtZShould he---.1 Free Lending Library— a,Fhtd the second stage, and we trust ' '°!Ls the year clos,-ts we shall be in a to say that it has reached the third in fact, triumphant. Councillors PIERPOINT, and H. ROBERTS

rendered the agitation great service, on Tues- day, by bringing the question before the Town Council. It was a matter of course that op- position should be encountered; but as they have right on their side, and the facts in their favour, they have • but to persevere to convert a minority into a majority, Al- derman HARRISON, who recently acted as Deputy Mayor, was the chief opponent of the project; and as, like Councillor PIERPOINT and Councillor BOLTON, he is a member of the Library Committee, it is due to him that what he has advanced should be considered. He professes to be in favour of a Free Lend- ing Library, providing the financial difficulty can be got over; but, if he is a friend of the movement, we can only say that, judg- ing from his conduct in the chair at the Town's Meeting and from the speech he made in the Town C9uncil, he has, unfortu- nately, a very unfriendly way of expressing himself. He contends that the ratepayers are pledged by the resolution passed under the Public Libraries Act of 1850 to support d Library, Museum, and School of Science. But if this resolution is so terribly binding, how is it that it is not being carried out ? Where is the "School of Science" about which he speaks? We know of no such in- stitution carried out under the Libraries• Act in Warrington; it is a figment of the imagi- nation—a castle in the air. Alderman HAR- RISON knows, or ought to know, that what the Burgesses did in 1850 was to adopt the Act; and that by it and subsequent Acts that have been passed they have the power to establish a Public Library which shall be a Free Lending Library. It is too late in the day to suggest that Warrington cannot do, under the Act, what has been done by every town by which it is surrounded—by, in fact over one hundred towns in the 'United Kingdom. If there is any irregu- larity or illegality, it is in making a charge for the loan of books which, according to I the letter and spirit of the law, should be lent, if they are -lent at all, " free of all charge." From the inquiries we have insti- tuted, we believe we are right in saying that Warrington is the only town in the United' Kingdom which makes a charge for the loan of books from a so-called Free Library. It is I sheer mockery to say, as Alderman HARRI- SON does, that "so far as a Free Library was concerned, they possessed one in the fullest acceptation of the term." The fullest ac- ceptation means that the ratepayers shall be free to borrow, and without any charge, the books which have been purchased by the ratepayers' money, as is done in Manchester, Liverpool, Southport, St. Helens, Wigan, Runcorn, &c. The inhabitants are reminded that they can, if they choose, "take advantage of a comfortably furnished room, well warmed, and well-lighted." Just so; nobody disputes , that; but if this " comfortably furnished ' room" is good enough for the "lower ' crust," how is it that it is not re- garded as good enough for the "upper , , crust?" What is sauce for the goose ' should be sauce for the gander, or even more aristocratic birds, when it is a question of carrying out the law. The world has moved on since 1850, and it is as well that Warrington should recognise in these days that, while a reading-room is useful for refer- ence books and periodicals, solid reading can best be done at home. The men who rule the roast will, of course, dispute this ; and, immediately afterwards, as privileged per- sons, they will tuck a ratepayers' book under the arm, and march off home with it. • But it is, after all, urged that the sole diffi- culty in the way of freeing the Library is one of money. Even Alderman HARRISON will be " mum " as to what was arranged some thirty odd years ago, if those who are agitat- ing in this matter will provide £7,000. He has a lively imagination; but that of Alder- man WEBSTER is livelier still, for he talks of ro,ooo as being required. It is a pity that neither of these financial authorities took the trouble to show why such a large sum would be needed to replace the loss of £133 a year in subscriptions. The omission was less ex- cusable on the part of Alderman HARRISON since he was challenged at the Town's Meet- ing to elucidate the mystery. No doubt the committee could spend the interest on to,ooo ; but that is quite another thing. The view we take, and have always taken, is that the committee must cut their coat accord- ing to their cloth. If they cannot get a sum capitalised to replace the income from subscrip- tions, they must do without it. The Library can be made a Free Lending Library this year, and that without closing either the Mu- seum or the Art Gallery. All that is required is that the committee shall practice retrench- ment—that as a means to live they shall live within their means. Twenty years ago—that is in 1867—, they managed to keep open both Library and Museum with £251 from the rates land £7l from subscriptions—a total of £322, as compared with the £530 which' is to be obtained to-day from the rates alone; or, to put it in another way, if the subscriptions I were abolished to-morrow the Library Com- mittee would still have an income to work ' upon of over £2OO per year more than they had in 1867. We therefore propose to show that, taking the accounts for last year as a basis of calculation, it would be possible to make ends meet without depending upon subscriptions. An estimate for the coming year framed as follows would dispense with the necessity of raising either £ to,ooo or £7,000

Total Expenditure 537 2 4 In framing the above Budget, .all we have left out, on the income side, from what was actually received last year is the "balance in hand,' the amount received from subscrip- tions, and an item of Li r7s zod for bank interest. Turning to the Expenditure side, 'we may explain that we have not touched salaries ' • but in the Museum Department we have knocked off [is 3s Bd, for "clean- ing cases and specimens." and k 293 4_s for "specimens, cases, Scc.," as items arising out of the recent alterations and improvements which will not occur again. In the Art Gallery Department and Library Department there is no reduction ; they are left un- touched; and it is the same with the Sink- ing Fund, for that is an item which must be met. The Establishment expenses are reduced bi£z 6 14.9 for painting, which is also an excep- tional outcome of the alterations, &c. The
