only other item left out is that of £76 9s zd for gas, which might be suppled by the Cor- poration free of charge, as is done, we under- stand, in some other towns. We thus get a " balance to the good," as the phrase is, of £3 i 13s 6d; which might be set aside for the extra wear and tear consequent upon the Library being brought for the first time into full use, by becoming a Free Library " in the fullest acceptation of the tem."

THE tidings of the death of Mr. PETER RYLANDS came upon the whole community with something of a shock, for his name was " familiar in our mouths as household words." It was rumoured that the painful strain of the last election contest, in which, through division in the Liberal camp, he had to meet as foes those who had formerly fought with him as friends, had seriously impaired his health ; but he was naturally so robust, so strong constitutionally, that, out- side a very narrow circle, it was not known until a fortnight ago that he was really in a critical condition. The news of his death was, therefore, a surprise to the public, but, coming as a surprise, it has been the means of intensifying the universal expression of I regret. Connected, as he has been, with Warrington from his birth, and rising by sheer force of character and ability until he successively occlipied the posts of Mayor and of Member for the Borough, it was no more than seemly that the Town Council should, ;at its meeiing on Tuesday, pass a vote of condolence, accomp inied with profound ex- pressions of regret for his loss. The loss, 'let us hasten to add, is more than local: it ,is a national loss ; for, if the late member for Burnley had been sparad to discharge his Iduties with the same assiduity as of old, his voice would have been heard with powerful effect in a Parliament which is likely to dis- tinguish itself by taking the first step towards I the reduction of our extravagant national expenditure. Mr. PETER RYLANDS had made ;the question of finance a special study ; he I desired to bring to the conduct of our national affairs the keen regard for economy which the members of the House of C.:om• mons, as business men, usually show in the I management of their own concerns, rightly be- lieving that, if this were done, many millions , of money might be saved, and that the burden of taxation would be pioportionately lighter. FL: also devoted considerable attention to ;foreign affairs, and, as a Radical economist, he was strongly opposed to the prolongation of hostilities in Egypt after the death of General GORDON. In this particular he was at issue with Mr. GLADSTONE'S Government, and it is due to his memory to say that the leading members of the Administration after- wards came round to his opinion. When the ; great controversy arose which split the Liberal party in two, Mr. RYLANDS. much to the surprise of those who were familiar with his speeches on Ireland, threw in his lot with , the Liberal Unionists ; and, as he was ener- getic in everything he took in hand, he was soon in sharp conflict with the majority of those who had formerly been amongst his' warmest admirers. Things were said by him, and of him, which had been better left un- said, and which we may now willingly let die, for, as •` CHRISTOPHER NORTH" once beau- tifully observed—" the animosities are mor- tal, but the humanities are eternal." It is in the spirit of this aphorism that the Conservative press acknowledged virtues in the sturdy Radical who had become a Unionist to which they had for a genera- tion been blind ; and it is in the same spirit that politicians of all shades will meet to-day with kindly hearts, and some, may with dimmed eyes, at the grave of the earnest and thoughtful man, who, as ducy called, spent the best years of a long public life in the ser- vice of his country and ,his kind.

I DEC-ruaz AT WIDNES.—In Zion Free Methodist Chapel en Monday evening, the Rev. J. Chisholm, of Liverpool, delivered a lecture on "Barking through the fence" to a good audience. The Rev. E. Hall presided. WIDNES ACCIDENT Hospirer..—At the monthly meeting of Widnes Local Board, on Tuesday, Mr. E. Carey gave no- tice that at the next mee.ting he should propose that the fee of ls per day charged for patients its the Accident Hospital be abolished. WIDNES SCHOOL BOARD AT WOHR.—Mr. U. H. Hanby, clerk to Widnes School Board, on Thursday brought a num- ber of persons before the magistrates fur neglecting to send their children regularly to scnoul. Ihe usual penalty of 53 was imposed in each case. THE REV. W. W. B. Onmsny, MA.—This rev, gentleman who wok the position of senior curate simultaneously with the new vicar of Runcorn, the Rey. A. Maitland Wood, has suddenly and unexpectedly taken his departure from the town. During his brief stay Mr. Ormsby made himself very popular with the parishioners, aud his disappearance has been the cause of much gossip. Tne explanation given is that his health suffered through the Runcorn atmospnere. AsSATILT oN THE POLICE AT WIS.—At Widnes Police Court, on Monday, Bernard Cullen, a labourer, Was charged with having on Saturday been drunk and disorderly, and assaulted P.C. Houghton. ConstMles Houghton and Wore- fold apprehended the prisoner and another man for being drunk and fighting in Wellington-street. Prisoner acted in a most violent manner, kicked Himghtou on the knee, and also struck him with his fist. The prisoner was ordered to pay 203 and costs or go to gaol for a niotnk THEFT BY A "CINDEit PICKEH' AT WinNes.—Before Mr H. liaskell, junr., and Mr. J. The prisoner was seen ivalkiug, from the yard with the wood in her possession, and else WAS sentenced to 21 days' hard labour, as eke had been previously wil- -1 victed.

1 " PRIMROSE " FESTIVITIES AT RuNcortx.—Last night, the members of the Rencorn Habitation of the Primrose , League gathered in the Public Hall to enjoy a few hours recreation. The Proceedings commenced with a tea pre- pared and dispensed by the "Dames" of the League, about 300 persons partaking of the good things provided. Subse- quently a concert was held, and later on the room was cleared for dancing, the music being supplied by Woods' qoadrille band. The refreshment departou,nt was under the control of Mr. R. Gorst. confectioner, High-street. DAMAGING THE MASONIC HOTEL, RUNCORN.—Before Mr. James Handley, J.P., aud Mr. G. L. Davies, at Runcorn Police Court on Wednesday, James Hewitt, a native of Warriogton, was convicted of having been drunk and disor- derly on Monday night in Devonshire Square, and with wilt oily smashing a plate glass window, worth £3 103, in the Masonic Hotel. The case was proved by the manager and Mr. 'Limas Lvdiate, and he was ordered to pay a total of £5 33 41, including damage, fines, and costs, or go to gaol for six weeks.

- LATE CANON BARCLAY, OF RUNCOON.—Miss Barclay has signified her intention of erecting a reredos in the chan- cel, at All Saints Parish Church, its a memorial to her lamented father. Tee necessary permisssion has been granted by the vicar and the partehinnere, and the execution of the work has been entrusted to Messrs. Pattison and Nor- bury. The reredos will be constructed of alabaster in the form of gothic arcades, and the subject represented will be the Ascension of our Lord. The cost .is estimated at £3OO It has also been decided to furnish the chancel with choir stalls, and to form a choir vestry near to the south door. P. Fletcher in the chair. In their report the directors stated that the gross profits amounted to £17,571 4s, from which had to be deducted office expenses, salaries. commissions, £4,731 153 41. The balefice from last year was £5,241 Os 7d, from which directors' fees (£1,000) were deducted. The available balance was therefore £17,380 9, 31, whish it was proposed to eppropriaie ass follows t—Dtvidend. 153 per share, £9,000; belaece carried forward, £8,380 93 3d.— The Chairman moved the adoption of the report. He also proposed a dividend, as fnemed, of 153.—Mr. J. Higson seconded both prooottels, whicp were adopted.—Mr. Hender- son congratulated (be shareholders on the satisfactory I charecter of the report. —lhe eetiring directors. Messrs. Charles Langton and E. W. Raynor were re-elected. BRUNSWICK IMPROVEMENT CLASS, RUNCOUN.-013 Wed- nesday evening time lady members took complete charge of the meeting of this society. Mrs. Wood took the chair at 8-15, in a crowded room. Glees were-efficiently rendered by Misses Jones, Simile, Crosby, and Eirkert, Miss E Wright presiding at the ;ilea°. The essays on "George Herbert" and" Leisure time" were read by Miss Leach and Miss I Walker (for Ms 9 Simkin) respectively. eleadings were given by Miss A. Littler, Miss Walker, and Miss Tyrie. Mies Lame Hayes recited "Billy's rose." The item of most importance was the trial scene from Shakespeare's "51er- I chant of Venice," with the following cast:—Portia. Miss Peacock ; Shylnek, Mike; Crosby; Duke, Miss Simeox ; Rae- sanio. Min 8 C. Littler; ISL:flees, Mire Cooke; and Gratiano, Miss E. Wright. After the most enjoyable evening spent ' for some seasons, a hearty vote of thanks was passed to the ladies for their entertainment, on the motion of Mr. J. D. Jones. seconded by Mr. F. J. Norman, the proceedings ter- minating with the doxology. Pafiustose LEAGUE MEETING.-0a Monday evening a well-attended meeting of the League and friends was beld in the Halton Girls' School. The following resolution, moved by the Ruling Councillor (Rev. J. Lockwood), and seconded by Mr. J. W. Haddock, was passed That this meeting de,ires to express its very great regret at the un- avoidable absence of Lady Brook, owing to the recent seri- ous illness of Sir Richard, and would venture to convey to I her ladyship and family their deep sympathy and earnest I hope that Sir Richard may be speedily restored to health." Mr. Molvneux Seel, the primrose agent for this district, proposed "That this meeting of the Halton Habitation de- clares its confidence in Lord Salisbury and her lelajeetY's Ministers. and records its full approval of their past and present policy."—This was seconded by Mr. T. Fielding. of Manchester, who, in a vigorous address, dealt with the sub- ject of Home Bale. During the evening various songs were rendered. The proceedings closed with the singing of. the National Anthem. A WALK FROM HALE CHURCH AND ITS RESULTS.—At Widnes Petty Sessions, oh Thursday, James Worrell, 18 years of age, who resides with h.s parents in Smith-lane, Speke, was charged with having on Sunday. the 30th January, iedecently assaulted Mary Southern, 19 years of age, who resides with her widowed mother at Speke. Mr. J. 0. Swift defended. On the evening of the Sunday named the complainant went to Hale Church. As she was returning home along Hale-road after the service she was overtaken by the defendant, who walked alongside for some time, and commenced a conversation. At length the pri- soner attempted to throw her to the ground and acted in an indecent fashion. She threatened to tell his mother, and he offered her 2s not to do se, but she refused the money. The defence was that the defendant had known the com- plainant all his life, and on the evening in question walked along with her with his arm mend her waist. When they arrived at his father's house he kissed her and said "Good night." The accusation of indecency was denied. The Bench contrairtr d the defendant to the sessions for trial, but allowed bim out on bail.

- A. SUICIDAL MANIA.—Early On Thursday morn- ing, Ellen Smith, wife of James Smith, collier, of Ashton, and mother of seven children, attempted to destroy herself by cutting her throat with a razor. The poor woman hid been unwell NI- some time, and had been attended by Dr. Latham. She had become low-spirited, and, seizing her opportunity, she went downstairs in her husband's absence, and finding his razor, inflicted an awful gash in her throat. As soon as she was discov.eted a doctor was summoned, and her injuries were attended to. She lies in a precarious condition.—James Bate, aged seventeen, the son ot a Golborne publican, who cut his throat with a large carving knife in his father's 'house on the 26th ult., died from the in- juries on Thursday morning. - • • -.

THE Sam CANA.L COMPA—NY.—At the adjourned meeting of shareholders of the Manchester Ship Canal Company, held on Thursday, the new direc- tors—Lord Egerton of Tatton, Mr. W. H. Houlds- worth, M.P., Mr. J. K. Bytheil, Mr. C. Galloway, and Mr. Charles Moseley—were unanimously re-elected. Lord Egerton received a cordial welcome as the new chairman of the company, and in the course of a brief address said he could not refuse to take part in an undertaking which he believed to be of in- estimable benefit to Manchester, and which, he held, was capable of being brought to a successful issue if it only received on its merits the support of the people of this district and of the country at large.- Mr. John Hicks was re-appointed auditor to the company, and the meeting concluded with a 'hearty vote of thanks to Sir J. C. Lee (who presided) for his great services. THE MURDER OF A WARRINGTON PRIEST. At the Liverpool Winter Assizes on Tuesday, before Mr. Justice Hawkins, a man named Samuel Dalzell, forty-eight years of age, and described as a labourer, was brought up on an indictment charging him with having, at Satan, on the Bth of December, caused the death of a priest named George Newton. The prisoner and Newton, it will be remembered, were inmates of the Rainhill Asylum at the time of the occurrence, and for some unexplained reason the two quarrelled. A struggle ensued, during which tpe prisoner picked up a brush, with which he inflicled a fatal blow upon Newton's head. The prisoner replied in a very excited tone that he was and went on to make a lengthy, incoherent statement, in which he complained of all manner of things, and charged the prison authorities with having severely illtreated him. Numerous oaths accompanied/ the prisoner's sta.ement, and each sentence Concluded with the appeal to his lordship, 'dye, understand? WIDNES AND THE LIVERPOOL WATER SCHEME.

Yesterday afternoon a special meeting of the Widnea Local Board was held for the purpose of considering the Liverpool Waterworks Supplementary Bill, and if thought proper, affixing the seal of the Board to a petition ti Parlia- ment. Mr. F. H. Gossage presided, and there were present —Messrs. Carey, T. Handley, Heyes, Taylor, S. Sadler, and J. T. Allen (clerk.)—At the request of the Chairman, the Clerk explained that as requested by the Board, he had consulted Mr. Oppenheim, solicitor, St. Helens, with regard to the rwasore, so that the Board would be in a position to watch the bill whilst it was in committee, to prevent any alte:ation being made in the agreement which had been entered into betweea the Board and the Liverpool Corporation. If tbe Board did not petition it was just possible there ml zbt be strong opposi- tion against the bill on the part of several local anthoritiee in the district, and this might result in a variation in the original argeement exieting between the Board and the Cor- poration which the Board had obtained at considerable ex- pense in years gone by.—Mr. Hayes quite agreed with Mr. ppenbeim, and the Chairman took the same view.—lt was unanimously decided, on the motion of Mr. Carey, seconded by Mr. Heyes, that the seal of the Board be affixed to a petition to Parliament in regard to the hill,and that Mr. Oppenheim be empowered to take such steps as be thought desirable to protect the interests of the Board.

ACCIDENT TO A RUNCORN SHUNTER.—A man named John Booth, who lodged with Mr. Peter Breton. Penketh-lane, Runcorn, met with serious injuries on Monday night at Atherton. Booth was a breaksman, and was in charge of a mineral train between Widnes and Bolton. div.head: WIDNES PARIS El CHURCH TEA PARTY.
div.p: WIDNES PARIS El CHURCH TEA PARTY.

The annual parochial tea party in co;;;Cti-oir ;i-t1; Widnes Parish Cnnrch took place on Wednesday evening, in the National Schools. About 500 persons sat dowu to tea pro- wiled by the ladies of the congregation ; and this number was considerably augmented a the subsequent concert, when Mr. T. C. Cdwards-Mess, M.P., occ,pied the chair. The Vicar, the Rev. J. Wright Williams, made a few brief remarks upon the parochial labours of last year, and said there was Yet a great deal to be done at St. Mary's and St. Paears.-t-The Chairman, who was enthasiastx ally received, said that in these days they had no right, nor was it politic for them as Churchmen, nor was it in the interest of their church, that they should not work together with those other religious denominations,which existed around them. (Applause.) They ought to recognise that they all had the stale aim in view, and were interested in the same questions of education, temperance, and morality, although working in different ways. (Applause.) It WAS well, he remarked, that the church was in a flourishing condition, because they could not tell how soon they would have to collect their forces in her defence. There was no knowing how soon the question might be asked of the country—"ls the church to be disestablished or is it not?" There were some who would like to abolish the church rather than reform it, but he was one of them who would rather mend than end it. (Applauso.)—The concert then proceeded. RUNCORN BURIAL BOARD. GREAT REDUCTION IN FEES.

The monthly meeting was held on Wednesday, Mr. W H. Rogerson, the chairman, presiding. Present —Messrs. J. Handley, J.P., E. Imison, W. Whittaker, W. Littler, H. H. Coleburn, G. Moss, R. Morris, and W. F. &likeld (sec- retary.)

It was reported by the Finance and General Purposes Committee that at a special meeting, held on the 14th Jan- uary, the Rev. A. Maitland Wood, M.A vicar of Runcorn, attended by rtquest in order that the committee might ex- plain to him the altered position of the Board with regard to burial fees, consequent on the death of the late vicar. A letter dated September 13th, 1886, from the Rev. W. Pres- ton, M.A , vicar of Holy Trinity Parish, was read claiming fees on interment of persons dying in his district. A let- ter was ales read from the Rev. ,J. Lockwood, vicar of Hal- ton, claiming fees for officiating at the funeral of one of his parishioners buried in the cemetery. The Chairman also exelained to Mr. Wood that in the opinion of the Bond the grave fees and monumental fees claimed by the clergy were oppressive to those who had graves in consecrated ground, that they operated against the ass of that portion of the cemetery, and against the erection of monuments. The Board considered that the time had arrived when this class of fees should cease to be levied. Mr. Wood, in reply, said that before he accepted the living the patrons had been informed there wae an income of £6O per annum from fees. He doubted whether he had power to give up any portion of the revenee, however willing he might be, but he would consider the matter and give an early reply. At a second meefing of the committee, held on the 4th inst., the Vicar again attended, and informed the committee that the Rev. W. Preston's claim to burial fees for his district was valid. The Vicar of Halton, however, had no claim to fees, the township of Halton not baying contributed to the cost of the cemetery. As regards monumental tees, it was not in his poem, to di,scorvinue them, but he had the power to revise them to such a point as they thought would be satis. factory to the ratepayers. After consideration the commit- tee decided provisionally to accept the compromise, and reduced the fees as follows: Fur a brick grave of one breadth For
£.d. .from 2 2 to 0 10 6
or vault of double

breadth „ 5 5 to 1 1 c For opening a vault For erecting a tomb with or without rails „ 5 5 to 1 1 0 For a atone on pillars, 3 feet In width 2 2 to 0 10 6 For a ledger or flalsoue „ 1 1 to 0 5 0 For a headstone F.r a mural monument in the chapel „ 5 5 to 1 1 0 The chsirmau was authorised to submit the revised list to the Vicar.

At a meeting of the committee held that day (February 9th) the chairman (Mr. G. Moss) reported that he had as requested submitted to the vicar the proposed revised list of fees, which the vicar agreed to. The chairman also read a letter from the Rey. W. Preston, M A., vicar of Holy Trinity, who stated that he was quite willing to " sc. quiesce in any suitable adjustment which Mr. Wood and the Board may judiciously determine upon." The com- mittee now unanimously recommended that from the date of the death of the late vicar the Board should charge fees on the revissd scale, and that the secretary should at once pay over to the respective clergy the fees in hand. Mr. Moss proposed, and Mr. W. Littler seconded, the adoption of the minutes, and the motion was unanimously agreed to. There was no other business of public interest.

div.head: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: WIDNES LOCAL BOARD.

The monthly meeting was held on Tuesday. Mr. F. H. Gossage, J.P., presided, and there were present, Dr. O'Keeffe, M ears Carey, Handley, W. W. Gossag., Mid- wood, Heyes, Taylor, Houghton S. Sadler, J. T. Allen (clerk), Carr (gas engineer), Higginson (surveyor).

div.head: -GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. -•
div.p: -GAS AND WATER COMMITTEE. -•

The minutes of this committee contained a report of the Gas Engineer, who said on the 11th January the Gasworks yard was fhoded to within 81 inches of the recent flood line. It commenced to show above yard gullies about six p.m., and continued to rise until midnight. Fortunately the water was slow in rising, which gave them time to set up temporary embankments of clay across the lower parts of the yard, which kept water out of the tar well and syphons, otherwise serious damage would have again re- sulted. As it was the damage amounted to about £l6. Extension of Carlfronizing Plant: It would, the Surveyor reported, be necessary during the coming season, besides do- ng the ordinary renewals, to erect some additional retorts, as the demand for gas was now within 15 per cent of their total producing power. From 1880 to 1883 there we a gradual falling in the quantity of gas concerned, but from 1883 to 1888 it had Increased 2.0 per cent. There were two schemes by which the necessary provision may be made. First the erection of a bed of retorts-14 mo uth eces—i n the peons at the north sod of No. 2 Rouse. This would cost about £250, and would meet an increased demand at a pro- portionate rate, for three years. The one objection to this proposal was that it would stop a useful passage, and make the work more cramped. The other scheme Was the recon- struction of the "Old." or No. 1 Retort House. This would give 56 additional retorts, and would increase the carboniz- ing power about 70 per cent, or otherwise meet a propor- tionate increasing demand for 10 or 12 years to come. The estimated cost was £1,676, exclusive of new aiding branch, which would reduce the cost of carbonizing considerably. During the laet month they had only one spare bed of re- torts, and if the c msumption of gas increases, of which there was every probability, this also may be required next winter. It was therefore of the greatest importance that he should have instructions to proceed with one of the schemes, for to work with a less margin than they had at present meant endangering the supply of as to the Itownship. The committee recommended that the scheme suggested by the engineer, estimated to cost £250 be adopted. The mean rainfall for the past month had been 2 920 inches. The illuminating power of the gas was 17 63 candles.—The tender at Robert Vt'atkinson for the supply of band reel and hose at £7O was adopted.—The minutes were passed, on the motion of Mr. Taylor, seconded by Mr. Sadler.

BIBCIMIELD•ROAD. The minutes of the Highway Committee contained the following remarks with regard to Birchfield-road :—The Clerk reported that be and the surveyor had had an inter- view with Mr. Young's agent (Mr. E. Wood), and that Mr. Wood had suggested that certain fencing should be done at once in lien of the work as per agreement Ist September, 188 T. Letter, 17th January, from Mr. Young's solicitor, Inquiring as to this suggested work, so as to cancel engage- ment. Recommended that the aforesaid agreement be cancelled up„ Mr. young agreeing thereto, and that the fencing, ttc., suggested by Mr. Wood, be done. At a subse- quent meeting a letter was read from Mr. Young's solicitor (B. Platoons), agreeing to cancel the unfulfilled portion of the agreement, let September, 1877, provided the new arrangement is at once carried out. In mov- , log the adoption of these minutes, Mr. Carey ex- plained that Mr. Young was the proprietor of the land in the neighbourhood of that road, and in 1877 an argument wee entered into to have the road widened, Mr. Young giv- ing 2,200 square yards of land, and the Board undertaking to make the road and put up certain fencing. Mr. Young did his part of the work, but at that time the prospects of Widnes were very much brighter than they had been since, and no doubt the Board thought the widening of the road would be a very g'eat and immediate advantage. Since then, however, the Board had thought that an expenditure of £l,OOO which would be involved was considerable, and that it would be a long time before the road was wanted, at a width of 42 feet. Mr. Young and his solicitor had been pressing the Board for four or five years to fulfil the agree- ment, but it bad been postponed from time to time in eon- twopence of the excessive expense. Be was glad to say „ that Mt. Young had consented to cancel the agreement on

consideration of certain fencing being done. Mr. Young had met the committee in a fair mad extremely liberal man- ner, because he could easily have foroed them to do the work and spend the money, and the Board owed him thanks for his kindness. (Hear. hear.) Mr. Allen informed him that the money they would have in hand after executine this work they would be able to spend in other parts of the township in more need of improvement, such as the prome- nade, and one or two other places.—Mr. S. Sadler seconded the motion, which was carried.

div.head: ABDUCTION O A CHILD FROM PENKETH.
div.p: ABDUCTION O A CHILD FROM PENKETH.

In the Chancery Division of the High Court of Justice, London, on Thursday, Mr. Justice North heard the petition of the mother for the restoration to her custody of her daughter, Ada Crookes, aged three and a half years, whom she alleged had been forcibly taken away from her by the father, Geotge Crookes. _

According tethe petitio,ner's story, she was mar- ried to George Crookes in 1876, and their first child I was born in 1880, but died two years afterwards.' The second child, Ada, was born in 1883. In 1885 her, husband bound himself to manage for seven years an engineer's business in Marcia, Spain, and, as she re- presented, insisted upon her going with him, tell- ing her that the climate would kill both her and the child. She stated that dur- ling the whole of her married life he had kept her shfirt of the necessaries of life, I but soon after she arrived in Murcia she and the child became seriously ill, and in August, 1886, she, with the child, returned to England, since which time she had lived with her father at Penketh, and had been entirely supported by him. Till February 2nd she was under the impression that her husband was still in Spain, but between two and three o'clock in the afternoon of that day, there was, she said, a knock at the door, and the child went to open it. Immediately afterwards she heard the child scream, and ran to see what was the matter. She found that her husband had seized the child, and that he had with hini his brother and another I man. She endeavoured to get possession of the, I child, and her father, an elderly man, came to her assistance, but was knocked down 'in the struggle. Mr. Cozens Hardy, Q.C. (with him Mr. Leonard Field), now stated that he was in possession of strict proof of service of the petition on Monday last, at ten o'clock in the morning, and the order blade on that day was at once telegraphed to Shef- field. Crookes' father had also been served. From in- quiries made at Bridlington Quay Station, it was found that George Crookes left there at half-past seven on the same morning with his " mother for Sheffield, and the mother was seen to return in the evening alone. ,On the same day a solicitor at Shef- field went to the residence of the brother there, but found the house closed, and on visiting. another house in Sheffield, to which he was informed the landlady of the brother had removed, he made inquiries ot her, and she admitted that George Crookes and the child slept at her house on the 2nd of February. He afterwards, at another house, found the brother, who admitted that he assisted George Crookes in the abduction of the child. Mrs. Crookes, he was informed; brought the , child to Sheffield from Bridlington Quay, and returned the same day, leaving the child at Sheffield. Mr. Justice North ordered the infant to be de- livered to the mother, and to remain in or under her control till further orders. The decision bas given great satisfaction in Pen- keth and Warrington, where the parties to the suit are well known. 7 '

div.head: WARRINGTON RAGGED SUNDAY SCHOOL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RAGGED SUNDAY SCHOOL.

This school, the establishment and objects of which have previously been described in these col- umns, progresses in its good work, and every Sun- day the large room is almost filled by an army of youngsters who have begun to look forward to the Sunday afternoon gathering. Last week a new de- parture was made, for on Saturday a free tea was given to the ragged children of the town, who poured in from all *quarters to the number of over four hundred. Every preparation had been made for them, and though their number was so large, none were agowed to go away unsatisfied. Indeed, some thirty others, who were found to be standing outside the building after the tea, were also sup- plied with cakes and oranges, of which a good, sup- ply had been laid M. The arrangements made for feeding all those hungry little ones were simple, but very effective. A large quantity of cakes and buns had been portioned out in paper bags, and most of the children brought with them mugs or cups out of which to drink their tea. After they had all been arranged in their places—and a very orderly set of children they ,were considering their circumstances—a bag of eatables was distributed to each one, and as soon as possible afterwards the tea urns wore brought round, and then for a time the children addressed themselves seriously, to the business in hand, and made short work of the good things provided. Although the clothes of most of them were as ragged and tattered as usual, a distinct improvement rn their appear- ance since the school was first commenced was noticeable in one particular. That was that their hands and faces were decidedly clean; there was scarcely a dirty face amongst them. To effect this radical change the management of the school had adopted the plan of presenting the children who attend the school with tablets of soap, Mr. John Crosfield having sent a nice present of 400 tablets of "Perfection." For a time the voluntary waiters who looked after the wants of the visitors were kept hard at work, but gradually their labours de- creased as the children's appetites became satisfied. After tea was over, and grace had been Raid, a few suitable words were addressed to the children by -by the Rev. O. E. Cutting, who had entered the room while the tea was proceeding, and by the Superintendent, Mr. Skelland, both of whom were enthusiastically cheered. Cheers were also given for those who had assisted at the tea, and those who had helped to provide it. Afterwards the children,n.s they filed one by one out of the room, were each given an orange, and went on their ways rejoicing. The oranges had been purchased from some of the vendors in the market, who kindly 'contributed a considerable quantity at their own cost. rue fol- lowing ladies and gentlemen were present, and rendered valuable assistance superintendent (Mr. J. Skelland), the secretaries (Messrs. W. H. Butler and IL Osborne); the teasurer (Mt R. Dale) ; and the following teachers and friends: The Misses Brown, the Misses Dale, the Misses Skelland, Mrs. Dale, Mrs. Osborne, Miss Cox, Miss Ashworth, Miss Miss Wallington, Mrs. Thomas, and Messrs. Steele, Adams, Owen, Healey, Ashworth, and Thomas.

After tea an entertainment was given in the Town Hall, consisting of vocal find instru- mental music' recitations, and the following dialogues : ' The teetotal barber," "John Mason's rercue," and " A couple of young ducks." An excellent and humorous ad- dress was given by Mr. C. Hodgson, of Calford High Trea- surer of the order, bearing on Rechabitistn. The Rev. A. P. Reynolds, M.A., vicar of Kingsley, presided.

div.head: VOLUNTEER FUNERAL AT ST. HELENS.
div.p: VOLUNTEER FUNERAL AT ST. HELENS.

The remains of the man named John Connison, of 28, Croppei's-hill, St. Helens, who was killed at Widnes last week, were interred •,t Eccleston Churchyard, on Saturday afternoon, and the Carrera', owing to the deceaseo's connec- tion with the voluntk,r movement, was of an impressive character. The deceiteed was a sergeant of the 2nd Volun- teer Battalion of the South Lancashire Regiment, and was held in general respect among his comrades. About 120 (Zees and men gathered at tbe head-quarters of the bat- talson, the Volunteer Hall, St Helens, and the C Company of the regiment providtd a firing party of 18 men and one corporal. under the directions of Sergeant Thchards. 1 11, baud of the regiment was in attendance u ti&r the conductorship of Band- master Arkell. Lie volunteers, under the command of Major Brown, who was accompanied by Major MaTear, and Lieutenants Cook aud Thou.son, marched to the de- ceased's late residence, where they arrived about three o'clock. Here a large number of spectators were congrega- ted. The mournful proceasion was beaded by the firing party of voluwee-s, who were succeeded by the band. The latter were foflowed by the hearse and tt ree mourning coaches, containing relatives and itnm-diate friends of the deceased. Following wore a numLer of the worktnen from the foundry of Messrs. Robinson and Cook, by whom the deceosed was employed at the lime of his death next in mder was the general body of volunteers, and the rear wan brought up by theofilicers present. As an additional mark of respect for the deceased volunteer, the coffin containing his remains was covered with a Union Jack, and the helmet fcrmerly worn by Connison' with his side-arms, in addition to a large nucnber of wreaths. Along the route the band rendered the" Dead March "from "Saul," and on arriving at Fccleslon Church, the firing party lined the read, the band rendering Beethoven's "Funeral Moon " in an affect- ing manner. The funeral service was conducted by the vicar, the Bev. B. EN Clarke, MA. At the conclusion of the graveside porting of the service three volleys were fired over the grave, the and rendering an appropriate selection .between each volley. The little conntry church was crow- ded by a sympathetic congregation.

div.head: LATE MR. IMA.DBENT.
div.p: THE LATE MR. IMA.DBENT.

At the close of a special sermon at Cairo-et. Chapel, Warrington, on Sunday morning, the Rev. R. Filcher, 8.A., referred to the lamented death of Mr. C. Broadbent. In his sermon he traced man's concep- tion of God through the three stages of develop- ment—force, mere intelligence, and love. He con- tinued :—I need hardly say that in all this I have had in mind the passing onward from our midst of an old benefactor of this ancient house of prayer, and an old worshipper within its walla. Seldom have I felt more deeply and strongly the comfort of our faith in our Heavenly Father, which has been the unvarying theme of its preachers for nigh upon two centuries. The pitiful and over-urgent appeals for mercy which fell upon my ears last Thursday sink for me awed and rebuked, in the presence of Eternal Dive. In God we live, and move, and have our being, and in the love of God we may rest secure. There are many will now hear me who knew Mr. Broadbent far longer, and therefore better, than I could or did, and who, if it were needful, should speak of him here instead. of me. The number of men and women who gathered to pay their last tribute of respect at his grave, and the wide diversities which they represent4l in theology, in politics, in social station, and in individual peculiarities, prove that there was in him—unveiled, if sometimes veiled by human frailties—a love which was akin to the Divine love, and which shared in its binding as well as its attracting power. He was closely allied by ancestral ties to this house, wherein many generations have met to worship, and he could not but be proud of it and its history. Nor can its members, knowing his past labours in its interests, Ibe anything but proud of him. Faith that worketh —and that worketh in love, represents the spirit upheld in our sanctuary, and set forth in his life. We thank God, therefore, for whatever was good in him, and surrender him -with full trust into his Father's hands, who will make even what was not so good to yield His venerable praise. Nor less do we commend to the Father's keeping the widow and children that lament his loss. Neither he nor they can be where God is not: and where He is we are sure there is safety, and there the everlasting peace. May that peace be theirs, that when the first natural flood of grid is past they may be up- lifted and strengthened in that love of God which makes one the great family which calls him,Father, part of which still dwell in these earthly scenes, and the larger part of which dwells in His more immediate presence, in the bosom of His love, now , and for evermore.

div.head: FIRE AT HOWLEY QUAY. WARRING-
div.p: FIRE AT HOWLEY QUAY. WARRING-

TON.—DAMAGES £2,000. A fire broke out on Sunday morning at the pre- mises of Messrs Hutchings, tanners, Howley Quay, . which resulted in considerable damage being done to the building and stock. The fire was discovered by 'a postman named Ellam, who, when on his round delivering letters in the neighbourhood of Howley, noticed smoke issuing from a stove room over the engine house. The foreman of the tan- ner?, Joseph Forster, lives near, and the postman gave the alarm to him. The services of several other workmen were immediately obtained, and in- formation was given to Police-sergeant Bowen, who rang the,fire bell. Mr. Frank Turner, superinten- dent of fhe Fire Brigade, and the whole of the fire- men, witd one exception, quickly answered the call, and, with the steam engine "Major," were in a very short time at the scene of the fire, and ac- tively engaged in suppressing it. A good supply of water was obtained from the river near at hand,and by strenuous efforts the brigade succeeded in con- fining the fire to the building in which it had broken out, thus saving much valuable property. The superintendent, the deputy-superintendent, the engineer, and the whole of the men worked hard and with a will for several hours, and too . much credit could not be accorded them. The stove-room where the fire broke out is on the second floor of the building, and underneath it is the engine-house. On the right and on the left hand, and also behind, are somewhat extensive buildings, in which the various processes in the , tanning business are carried on. The walls on the left, and behind, are fire proof. In the stove-room a considerable number of hides, or pieces of leather. approaching the finishing stage, had been placed a short time before. They were estimated to be worth about „CI each, and numbered between 450 and 500. As most of them were destroyed it will be seen that considerable loss was sustained in ad- dition to the damage done to the building. By the time the fire brigade had reached the place the flames had got firm hold of the stove-room, and the firemen looked to saving the other property. Beyond slight damage done to an adjoining-room& on the right the fare was confined to the stove-room, which,. in the space of two hours, was reduced toadies: The roof was entirely cleared away, and nothing was to be seen from the outside except the framework of the buildihg, the beams and uprights of the building., which were scarred to such an extent as to render. ' them utterly useless for any further service. The timber floor of the room was to some extent ren- dered fire proof by the water falling upes . it, but it also was damaged tea great extent, and the. machin- ery underneath was also materially inpared by the water which went on it. Some machinery in the. stove room fell through to the room beneath, in- creasing the damage. Altogether it is estimated. that damage to the extent of £2,000 was occasioned. It is covered by insurance in the " Queen's" Com- pany. A large number of people witnessed the conflagration, and several police officers, including- Sergeant Shaw, Constables Bowen and Wheatley, were present to keep order.

THE LATE MR. WARRINGTON WOOD. The TOWN CLERIC read the following letter:—" 78, Sloane-street, January 31, 1887. Dear Sir,—l beg to ac- knowledge with sincerest thanks and gratitude the beautiful and touching tribute paid by the Town Council of War- rington to the memory of my beloved husbend. The sym- pathy manifested by his fellow-townsmen tales been un- speakably precious to me, and this official t,etimony to his talents and worth is the meet precious of all, and one I shall never cease to treasure.-1 remain, dear sir, your obe- dient servant, AMELIA WARRINGTON WOOD." In - 1864 they made an important departure—important not less to the in- dustry of the town than to themselves as manufac- turers. Works were established in Warrington in the year just mentioned for the purpose of produc- , ing the puddled iron from which the wire was made, and, employment was given to a large num- ber of people. Ten years later the ironworks were amalgamated with those of the Dallam Forge Com- pany at -W arrington, and with the collieries of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles at Wigan. The new company went under the title of the Pearson and , Knowles Coal and Iron Com- pany, the capital was nearly a million, and the principal 'shareholders and directors were the former partners. The enormous extent of the collieries et this company is well known through- out Lancashire. Coal and cannel have been pro- duced to the extent. in a single year of 400,000 tons. With regard to the manufacture of iron wire, with bars, plates, sheets, hoops, &ea the development under the new condition of things was remark- able. It is not too much to say that the growth and prosperity of Warrington ,is due to no small extent to the energy and success of Messrs. Rylands Brothers. Mr. Rylands, we may add, was also a, director of several important limited companies, in- , eluding Francis Morton and Co., of London and' Liverpool, manufacturers'of fencing materials andl galvanised iron buildings; the Manchester and ' Liverpool District Banking Company; the West Mostyn Coal and Iron Company; the Pearson and Knowles Coal and Iron Company, Limited; War- rington Wire Rope Company, Limited; of the Scottish Equitable, and vatious other commercial concerns. Mr. Rylands was ,twice married, his fires wife being Miss Ragg, of Ashby-Ide-la-Zouch, and has second, to whom he was ' married in 1861, was Caroline, daughter of the Itte Mr. W. Reynolds, of Fenketh House, Warrington, who, together with three sons and two 'daughters, survive his loss. Mr. McMinnies, J.P., it may be mentioned, married a sister of Mr. Rylands's first wife, and it need hardly be said that he feels keenly,the death of a man with whom he has been so long and intimately associated. . Councillor HOBERTS explained that he was not connected with the Free Library movement, and he had never spoken publicly no the subject before that night. lie had no right to ely what the promoters of the library scheme were going to do; be simply asherted that they might if they chose make it a leading question. (blear, hear, and a voice:" Let them do it then.")

Some might posshly wish to build a tall tower. (Laughter.) However, all there matters would be considered be the committee, and they would only be wasting their time by carrying the subj.,ct further. Alderman DAVIES called attention to the fact that the Liver- pool Dock and Barbour Boards were seeking to Cass a bill through Parliament which would materiallyaffect the navi- gation a the Mers,y so far as Warrington was concerned.— After some remarks by Alderman Cmosnntio, it was agreed that action should be taken to hay., two of the clauses of the propos-d bila altered before passing Parliament. This was all the business.

WARRINGTON TOWN POUNCIL. ELECTION OF MAYOR. On Tuesday evening a special meeting of the War- rington Town Council was held in the Council Chamber, Town Hall. for the purpose of electing a . Mayor of the borough La place of Dr. Mackie, who has resigned owing to illness. The Deputy-Mayor (Alderman Harrison) presided, and there were also present Aldermen Holmes, Burgess, Davies, Pickmere, Crosfield, Chandley, and Webster; Councillors Bar- ker, Brown, Jolley, Francronb. Dakin, Dixon, Greening,,lleaton, Bolton, Litton. W. Pierpoint. J. Pier- point, Fleming, Taylor, Wright, Roberts, Tinsley, Marsh, Taylor, Platt, and Ashton ; Messrs. Brook (town clerk), Whittle (deputy town clerk), Longdin (borough surveyor), Clas,rl.-y (borough treasurer), and Paterson (gas manager). The DEPUTY MAYOR brietly explained the object of the meeting, and remarked that thsy never met for the purpose of electing a Mayor under more mournful circumstances than those which characterised the event they were about to take part in. Alderman HOLMES then moved 'hat "Jahn Richard Pick- mere, Esq.. ose of the ald-irmen of this borough be, and is hereby duly elect d Mayor for the borough, to supply the vacancy occasioned by the resignation of Alexander Mackie Esq., and to continue in office so long as this said Alexander Mackie would have coniinned in office, viz, until the 9th day of Noventber,lB37, and until the acceptance of office by his successor." (Applause.) It was a fortunate thing for that Council, be said, that during the 39 years it had existed such a circumstance as the one under which they were met should net have occuraed before, and he hoped that the Corporation would last for another 39 years, or more, without having to go through a similar performance. (Hear. hear.) In seeking for a gentleran. upon whom con- siderable calls must be made,in cons.guence of it being the Jubilee year of her Majesty, they hid to find ono whose qualifications were excsptionally good; and he thought Alderman Pickmere would answer all the expectations formed of him. (Hear, hear.) It was not ask4cl that he should come down with a large sum of money to inaugurate any grand movement, but that he should lead them in any work they might endeavonr to carry out. If it should happen that the Queen. in the sxerclse of her royal prero- gative, should look down upon W +Airington as a town upon which an honour tniht be conferred. there was no gentle- man, and there was no lidy, upon whom the honour would better desco I than up,m Alderman and Mrs. Pickmere. (Applause.) Alderman DAVIES second-d the r.soltition. He referred to the uniform courtesy of Alderman Pickmere to all the members of the Council, and said that be would be only speaking the voice of everyone present when he said that they were glad to vote Alderman Picamere to the office of Mayor. (Hear hear.) He took that office under peculiar circumstances, and considerable difficulties, and only a man rased to the harness, who hail before been Mayor, would . have been able to do so at the present time. They should be glad that they had a man not only witting, but able to fill the office at a very delicate point in the life of the &Tore-

Lion. Alderman Burectese supportedlithe resolution. He wished, be said, to bear testimony to the qualifications of Alderman Pickinere for the office of Mayor. He did not think, con- sidering the year they were going through, that there was a member of the Council more adapted for the position, and one so well adapted to carry through the work that had tube done. (Hear, hear.) Circumsfances this year were of such a peculiar nature that at the outset they might say that they were under deep obligations to Major Pickmere for accept' lug the office. They all felt so confident as to the issue in Alderman Pickmere's hands that they could afford to anti- cipate a very successful Jabilee year in Warrington, al- though things had gone so adversely up to the present time. It was the duty of every member of the Council, and of loyal townsmen. to rally round him to help him to cele- brate the Jubilee year in a manner that would not only be satisfactory, but redound to the credit of Warrington. (Ap- plause.) Alderman CROSVIELD said they were undoubtedly placed in a peculiar position. Nothing could be sadder than the fact of Dr. Mackie being stricken down by sickness, when he had attained to the summit of his ambition; and under the circumstances he thought all of them, as well as the whole town, ware indebted to Alderman Pickmere for the self-sacrifice he had made in undertaking the duties of the Maverality for the remainder of the year. (Hear, hear.) He had not the slightest doubt that Alderman Pickmere would conduct himself as the Mayor of this borough during the Jubilee year of her Majesty the Qaeen as ably and as suitably as any &layer they could have found in England. (Applause.) The DEPUTY MAYOR said that he felt perfectly satisfied that the honour and credit of Warrington would be in sefe keeping in the bands of Alderman Pickmere, who, he knew, would do what was right. The resolution was then put to the meetieg, and carried unanimously. The MAYOR, in replying, referred to the painful illness of Dr. Mackie, and asked the committee to excuse him, as a mark of respect, from puttmg on the Mayoral robes that evening. (Hear, hear.) Warrington hod recently lost some of its worthiest sons, but he hoped that after sorrow joy would come, and that they should be able in the future to do something which should lsring the eld and loyal town of Warrington to its former statue. (Hear, hear.) He wil- lingly took office for one reason, that he believed the whole , of the members of the Council desired him to do so, and that his fellow townsmen outside the Council Chamber also wished it. (Applause.) There were men who were capable of fulfilling the duties of the office, and who might have undertaken it, but they declined principally because they : bad never occupied the chair before, and they thought the duties might be so arduous that they would not be able to carry them out to the satisfaction of the town generally. However, he had stepped into the breach, and it was his hope that he should have the assistance of the members of the Council, as well as of the town generally. (Hear, hear.) He purposed calling a meeting of the Council at an early day to form a "Jubilee Committee," and the influential gentlemen in the town would be called upon to assist in doing something which the majority of the people may think worthy of the good old town of Warrington. (A.p- plause.) He thank,nl them for the honour they had done him by electing him to the position of May cr. ADJOURNED COUNCIL MEETING. Immediately after the special meeting above reported a meeting of the Council adjourned from the previoui Tues- day was held to transact the ordinary business of the mantle The newly-elected Mayor ( Alderman Pickmere) presided, and the gentlemen whose names are given above were also present.

div.p: GRAPPENHALL PLOUGHING MATCH. A ploughing match, under the auspices of the Grappenhall Central District Ploughing Match Society, took place n land in the occupation of Mr. Richard Clark, known as the Millfield, Warburton, yesterday week. The lend was in very good condition, and on the whole appeared to suit the competitors. Some of the latter did their work extremely well, and the judges had no small difficulty in deciding upon their respective merits. The judges for the single furrow plough contests were Messrs William Cookson (Tarporley), William Hough (Mere), and Henry Bate (Saukey), while the competitions in the American Chilled ?tuna's were judged by Messrs John Baleen (Hale Bank), Thomas Baxter (Tarviu), and John Norimry (Ashley.) The three last named were also responsible for the awarding of prizes for the neatest and cleanest turnouts, &c. The total number of competitors Was 24, this number being rather less than lest match, which was held throe years ago The ploughmen met on the field for drawing lots as to position about eight o'clock, and the lend had to be ploughed at the rate of a statute acre in 14 hours, and any competitor who failed to complete his almtment in the specified time, would 'ee disqualified. The match appeared to excite a great deal of attention and interest, and there was a large attendance of speotatore. The judges, tho secretary (Mr J J Fairhurst), and other officials deserve every praise for the excellent manner in which they per- formed their duties. After the ploughing the ploughmen, with their friends, the officer,' of the society and other gentlemen adjourned to the Saracen's Head Inn, where an excel- lent tea was served by the host and hostess (Mr and Mrs Barff ) The chair was occupied by Mr William Derbyshire, of Grapnenhall, president of tho society, who was supported by the judges and other officials. After tea the list of prize winners was announced, and the prizes distributed to the successful competi- tors.-The CHAIRMAN, addressing the unsuccessful competitors, asked them to be satisfied with the deci- sion of the judges, who were gentlemen in whom they bad the utmost confidence, and there was no doubt they had awarded the prizes conscientiously and to the best of their ability. (Applause.) The secretary (Mr Fairhurst) announced the awards of the judges as follows CLASS 1, SINGLE FURROW PLOUGHS. (Open to all Reg- land).-let, Le, Richard Warburton, ploughman to Mr John Warburton, Grapoenhall ; 2nd, £4, Mr William Blackburn, owner end ploughman, Ashley, near Knuts- ford ; 3-d, £2, James Brown, ploughman to Mr John Brown, I Ashley. Crass 2, SINGLE FURROW Ptovems.-For men who have not won a first class prize, value £6, or a prize in. second class, value £6, within the last four years ;list prize open to all England, remainder for regular hired servants or mem- berg of the family of farmers residing in the Society's dis- trict: Ist. £5, John Renshaw. ploughman to Mr Richard Clark, Warburton Park; 2oel, £4, John Wright, lune., ploughman to Mr John Wright, sent., High Leigh : 3rd, £2. John Percival, ploughman to Mr Thomas Rigby, High Leigh; 4tl, £l, Peter John Leather, ploughman to Mr John Moore, Warburton. CLASS 3, SINGLE FURROW PLOUGHS.-For youths under 20, who have not won a first prize; first prize open to all England, and remainder restricted as in class 2. LONDON, MIIRSDIY. The debate on the Address still prevents com- mencement of public business in the House of Com- mons. Everyone denounces this mischievous ab- surdity ; yet there has never yet been failure made of a member from one side or the other to perpetuate it. Except when some speaker of high standing takes up the discourse. the House is miserably emply. Once Mr. Biggar attempted to take advantage of the situation by having the House counted out. But it is one of the most un- welcome duties of the whips that they are bound to "keep a House," so that the debate may reach a natural conclusion. Every night at question time you will see the junior whips going round the Con- servative benches with the monotonous question "Will you dine here to-night " ? • This does not mean an hospitable invitation to feed at the Go- vernment's expense. It merely expresses a desire that the person adel,--ed shall sacrifice his comfort and remain on the piemises through the sitting, with the purpose of defeating any of Mr. Biggar's little vagaries. If the member says " yes," his name is entered on the list. If he pleads another engagement, the whip goes elsewhere in search of a dinner brigade. An effort is made every night to get up a list of one hundred members to keep things safe. , This is really the most important and practical business of the successive nights. For the rest there is interminable talk round a foregone conclu- sion. Everyone knows that the Government will carry the Address by a considerable majority. Mr. John Morley and the great body of the Liberals will vote for Mr. Parnell's amendment; but the Dissentient Liberals will go into the other lobby; and thus the Government are absolutely safe. It is noteworthy that, according to present intention, Mr. Chamberlain does not mean to take part in the debate. He finds it easier to vote against Mr. Glad- stone than to argue in favour of Lord Salisbury. Writing a week before the session opened, I men- tioned a report that had reached me to the effect that Lord Randolph Churchill had threatened to leave the country before putting in an appearance at the House. I have no doubt that he threatened this, as he is accustomed in private conversation to make the wildest assertions. Ile, however, carried out the intention only in modified form, deferring his departure till after he had delivered a couple of speeches in the House of Commons.- That he should have gone to Algiers is rather an odd thing. Even at this early penod of the year the temperature on the southern Mediterranean shore is pretty high, and if there is one thing Iside Mr. Chaplin that Lord Randolph cannot stand it is hot weather. A good deal was said a month ago about a letter Lord Randolph had written to Mr. Akers-Douglas, the contents of which, it was assumed, would be made public. I believe Lord Randolph wrote the letter with a view to its ulterior publication. It was very long, giving in detail the reasons which led to his resignation. Perhaps the most important passages are those which define Lord Randolph's attitude towards the Conservative party. This he strictly and significantly limits to the question of union of Great Britain and Ireland. which, as it has never been in question, does not mean very much. Beyond this Lord Randolph plainly hints that the party have not much to expect from him unless they will follow his lead, and carry out that policy of retrenchment and non-intervention which Lord Randolph, with a shrewd appreciation of the situa- tion, has made his own. Upon these terms he gra- ciously announces his readiness to support his for- mer colleagues in office. That is to say, if they will do his bidding he will not attack them. If not, be does not say what will happen, but leaves it to the trained imagination of those who have sat with him in Cabinet Council or watched his conduct in the House of Commons. No one who saw Mr. Peter Rylands in the House of Commons at the end of last session could have I been much surprised by the sudden announcement of his death. He seemed to have fallen away in a remarkable manner, and though to the last lu..ur of his attendance upon the House he kept up his buoyant manner, it was rather painfully spasmodic. Politics were a serious thing with him, and I believe there is no doubt he felt the position when he found himself working for the advancement of the Conservatives to the despite of Mr. Gladstone and the Liberal party. Mr. Rylands was a staunch Liberal, even a Radical, and to have the last days of his political existence darkened by his "Unionist" connection could not fail to have effect upon his health and spirits. The approaching departure of the Queen to spend the freshest period of the London season on the Continent is this year greeted with a chorus of complaint more than usually loud. It is the Jubilee Year, and those persons more or less directly influ- enced by the locality of the Court think it might have been looked for as an act of grace on the part of her Majesty that she should celebrate the occa- sion by dwelling among her own people. But, really the Queen has, within the limits of her high posi- tion, as much right to follow her own fancy as any- one else. Moreover, if tke Queen were not at Aix- les-Bains, she would be at Osborne, or even at Windsor, which comes to much the same thing for the London tradespeople. The Prince of Wales has taken the opportunity of making holiday before the Queen sets out on her journey. He is to be back on the 28th, in time for the first levee, whilst the Queen does not start till a week later. _ News of another kind affecting the social habits of Monarchs comes from Berlin. The aged Emperor, who has always lived at home and forms part of the daily life of his capital, has been accustomed for more than a generation, at a particular hour of the day, to show himself at the window to his faithful people. As the hour approaches, the crowd gathers in the roadway—just as at noon in Cheapside there is always a throng standing gazing at Sir John Ben- net's clock awaiting the performance which accom- panies the proclamation of twelve o'clock. It is a pretty, simple, custom in accord with the character of the Emperor and of the German nation. The old Emperor comes to the window,- open in summer time; the crowd stand-uncovered and reverentally. gaze. Precisely to the appointed second, as he came the Emperor withdraws; the crowd re-covers itself,l and passes on fits way glad to have seen thel Kaiser. OUR FINANCIAL LETTER. [FROM OUR OWN CORRESPONDENT.] 23, Old Broad-street, E.C. The general tone of the Stock Exchange is much healthier this week than its predecessor if only on account of the absence of war rumours, and, prices having gone down to war rates last week, the upward movement was inevitable providing no further scares were started. The absence of general business, however, b still very marked, and prices were sent up rather for the purpose of the settlement than ' doe to any heavy buying and—the settlement having been brought to a conclusion—there is every probability of fur- ther sinister rumours for stock exchange purposes. It is al- most useless at the present time to quote priees of any stocks, the most steady going being subject to fluctuation at this time, but investors might do worse than devote some attention to home secnreties, especially railways, which at present prices offer a sound and profitable investment. Beer has been the chief interest of tha financial world, both Allaopp and Guinneas dividing attention, the former COM.. pany by the speculations as to how the allotment will be made, in view of a hundred millions having been applied for and only three millions to allot. The latter company has attracted renewed interest by the statutory meeting which was held thie week, and the subject of the allot- ment by Messrs. Baring was raised. The chief feature of interest, however, was the statement by the chairman that the company had purchased the plant, book debts for a sem differing from what the sharehold2rs' valuer and auditor made it by £.82,0000, whereupon the chairman at once drew a cheque and paid it to the company forthwith. A subject among many of vital importance was diem/teed at the annual meeting of the Associated Chambers of Com- merce, viz., the extension of Indian railways, which was moat heartily supported by the representatives of all the chambers.
PUBLIC BENEFACTRESS.

Mrs. S. A. ALLEN has justly earned this title, and thousands are this day rejoicing over a due head of hair produced by her unequalled preparation for restoring, in- vigorating, and beautifying:the Hair.

possibly succeed in converting Alderman Davies into a Liberal. (Laughter.) It would be a very considerable gain to their party, because he was a man of some influence, as they knew. (Laughter.) But there was this point to be also considered. They could not tell how long the present Govern- ment would last. They might be out in a fortnight or they might be out in two months. But let them imagine that the Government were to be defeated in a fortnight or three weeks and there was to be a general election. What would they do then? He should be between the Canary Islands and Jamaica, and he could not get back. But he wanted to tell them this—he wanted to give them perfect liberty, and if they thought it better to select another candidate in case of his absence—(" no, no,")—he should be perfectly satisfied. Let them not think he was at all thin-skinned, or that it would hurt his Ifeelings. He thought himself that the Government ' might possibly last through the session. (Hear, hear, and a voice: "What about making Sir Gil- bert a peer," and laughter.) Well, there was that to be considered. Sir Gilbert might be made a peer. For his own part he would not give is for all the titles the Queen could bestow—(laughter and ap- plause)—but he dare say Sir Gilbert hada little am- bition in that direction; and as far as he (Mr. Crosfield) was concerned, he should be very glad to see Sir Gilbert get:a peerage, because he thought he was much more suited for the House of Lords —(loud laughter)—than the House of Com- mons. Those of them who read " Toby's " remarks in "Punch" would remember that when Sir Richard Cross was made a peer he met Sir Richard in the lobby of the House, and congratulated him on his elevation. "I am very glad," said Toby, "to hear that you are going up to the House of Lords; it is exactly the place for you to go to." So he (Mr. Cresfleld) thought the House of Lords would be ex- actly the place for Sir Gilbert. (Applause and laugh- ter.) They all knew his political opinions pretty well, and he had no need to enlarge that night upon them. He was in favour of separating the Church from the State; he was in favour of denominational edu- cation. (Hear, hear.) He did not want a School Board in Warrington, with 2s in the pound added to the rates. (" No, no." "That is a mistake.") Well, he thought it would be 2s in the pound the first year; it might come down to Is in the second. But even is in the pound was too much, for he thought the rates of Warrington were quite heavy enough at present. (Hear, hear.) As he had said before, he thought it was a very great credit to Warrington to have maintained their schools out of their own pockets voluntarily. (Hear, hear.) He was sorrry if he could not agree with every one of them on that question; but he did not pro- fess to agree with every one. That was simply im- possible. (Hear, hear.) There were no two men in that room that had got the same heads on their shoulders, and their brains were all different. There- fore they got a lot of different opinion amongst themselves. (Hear, hear.) It was what they boasted of in the Liberal party that every man was free to exercise his own individual opinion. They were not like a lot of sheep, as the Tories were. (Laughter.) He had got those fixed opinions of his own, and as he said before, they would either have to take him with those fixed opinions or else they would have to do without him. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He thanked them most sincerely for the honour they had done him in selecting him as their candidate at the next election. (Loud applause.) The CrrAinueri said they were now "in for it," and whatever happened, and whenever it came, they would fight it to the death. (Applause.) He had no idea in his own mind that Mr. Crosfield would be absent when the election came, but ab- sent or present John Crosfield would be their mem- ber. (Loud applause.) , A vote of thanks having been accorded the chair- man, Mr. MCMINNIES, in responding, said the only thing he had to say was this—union, and they should be victorious. (Applause.) What made them victorious in 1880? They were all united, all earnest, all determined to win; let them be so at the next election. (Loud applause.) The meeting then ended.

The Mast;r of the Rolls announced in the Appeal Court' on Friday that Lord Justice Bowen, who kos been ill for some days, was unable any longer to sit in court, and had resigned. The strike among the glass-bottle makers of St. Helens was settled on Friday. The English workmen are to re- sume work on Monday. and arrangement' are being made ' for the Swedes. &c., to he sent home. A CLEVER FEAT.-Mr. Bullpet, of Oxford University, undertook, for a wager of three hundred pounds, to walk a mile, run a mile. acd ride a mile in eighteen minutes. He accomplished the feat in sixteen minutes, fifty-seven and four-fifths seconds. __

GREAT FIRE AT HULL.—A Ere broke out on Friday morn- ing at the oil mills of Messrs. Barton aud Waterhouse, Hull, the contents of which, consisting of oil seed and cake, were destroyed. damage ri the extent of between £30,000 and £4O 000 being done. The fire raged furiously for some [hours.

THE SPITALFIELDS DISASTER.—MT. Wynne Baxter, coroner for East Middlesex, on Friday summed up the evidence given in the inquiry into the cause of the deaths of persons who perished in the Spitalfields disaster. The jury returned a verdict of "Accidental death," but further ex- pressed an opinion that if the exit from the gallery had been in the same direction as the exit from the body of the hall fewer deaths would have occurred. THE SOUTHpORT MURDER TRIAL. At the Liverpool Winter Assizes, on Friday, before Mr. Justice Hawkins, Alfred Smith, sixteen years of age, was indicted for the wil- ful murder, at Southport, of a young woman named Maud Hamilton. on the 12th November last. The charge, after some evidence had been given, was reduced to one of man - Mang! The jury, without leaving the box, and after a few minutes' consultation, returned a verdict of " Man- slaughter, without intention to hurt," and strongly recom• mended the prisoner to mercy. The prisoner was sentenced to six months' imprisonment with hard labour. LAST NIGHT'S PARLIAMENT. HOUSE OF LORDS. The House met at 4 o'clock. DEFECTIVE WEAPONS.—The Earl of Heattownr asked whether there were at the Admiralty any complaints other than those mentioned yesterday of defective weapons sup- plied to the fleet 7—Lord ELPHINSTONE replied that all com- plaints by officers were Pent on to the War Office.—A schedule had been 'Anted, and was now in the hands of the War Office Commission. The House then adjourned. HOUSE OF COMMONS. The House met at four o'clock. Qtrwartores.—Sir M. HAMILTON. replying to Mr. Cony- bears, said Admiral Grant had caused lists to be circulated in Devonport Dockyard for subscriptions for the Imperial Institute, but no compalsion was used to secure contribu- tions.
