WARRINGTON LIBERAL COUNCIL. SPEECH BY MR. JOHN CROSFIRLD. On Monday evening a special meeting of the General Council of the Warnngton Liberal Council was held at the club, Bewsey-street, "to inform Mr. John Crosfield of the resolution passed at the last meeting of the General Council, requesting him to become the Liberal candidate for the borough, and to receive a reply thereto." The chair was taken by Mr. J. G. McMinnies, J.P,, and amongst the large number present were Alderman Burgess, J.P., Dr. Gornall, J.P., Rev. John Yonge, Rev. E. Moore, Messrs. r. A. Roberts, J. Winser, W. Pierpoint, H. Roberts, C. S. Burgess, J. Shaw Green, J. Walker, R. Roberts, &c. The CHAMMAN, who was received with applause, said he had peculiar pleasure in taking the chair that night for two reasons. In the first place be- cause he believed that the meeting would not be a prolonged one—(laughter)—and in the second place because there would be no controversial or disputed point introduced into their discussion. They had nothing to do but to tell their respected friend Mr. John Crosfield that they believed he was "their man." (Loud applause.) The Chairman then in- formed Mr. Crosfield that it had been resolved at the previous Council to ask him to be the Liberal candidate at the next general election. (Hear, hear.)' What Mr. Crosfield might have to say in reference to that he (the chairman) did not know, although he had a very good idea. (Laughter.) He had, however, now to ask Mr. Crosfield to res- pond in one way or another; " yea " or "nay." (Laughter and applause). Mr. CROSFIELD, on rising, was received with en- thusiastic applause. He said their chairman had remarked that he was going to preside over a short and pleasant meeting, and he (Mr.Crosfield) thought he would, because they knew very well that he did not like long speeches. Ile thought most men could say a good deal in twenty minutes, and if speakers generally would condense what they had to say there would be a great deal of time saved that was now wasted. (Hear, hear.) Well, he had a great want in his character—he was short of ambition. He had no ambition to go to Parliament, but if they thought he was the best candidate to fight, very well, he would fight. (Loud applause.) He had no fear of the next general election. (Hear, hear.) He thought the Tory party were in a miserably weak , condition, and the present Tory Government might go to pieces any day or any week. Lord Salisbury showed great weakness in his (Mr. Crosfield's) judg- ment, when he allowed Lord Randolph Churchill to kick Sir Stafford Northcote out of the leadership of the Tory party—(hear, hear)—and he made a still greater blunder when he took Sir Stafford North- cote's—then Lord Iddesleigh—office as Foreign Sec- retary, and so hurt poor Lord Iddealeigh's feelings to such an extent that it positively killed him. There was one newspaper said it was murder, but while he would not g 9 so far as that, it certainly affected Lord Iddesleigh to a terrible extent; and they could not imagine what his feelings must have ) been when he entered that room in the Foreign Office to meet Lord Salisbury. Lord Iddes- leigh was a gentleman that everyone respected— (hear, hear)—and he was worthy of respect ;he was a pure, upright,conscientious statesman, and he was a man that Englishmen might be proud of. (Hear, hear.) They were not narrow-minded bigots that they could not admire a man because he held dif- ferent political opinions from themselves, and he had always admired Sir Stafford Northcote, as he would rather call him. (Hear, hear.) Then Lord Randolph Churchill had also left the Tory Govern- ment, and he seemed to have been its prime mover. It was one of the finest things that ever happened in his (Mr. Crosfield a) life-time to see a Tory Chan- cellor of the Exchequer walk out of office rather than sanction that wicked and wasteful expendi- ture on the army and navy. (Loud applause.) They had been wanting that for a long while. The Tory party were the great spending party, and he remembered Mr. Gladstone telling him that he had no idea of the way in which the different depart- ments asked for more money. (Hear, hear.) He did hope that Lord Randolph Churchill's life might be spared, and that he might make his voice heard in the House of Commons and denounce extravag- ant expenditure. (Hear, hear.) Referring to Mr. John Bright, Mr. Crosfield said he went about a month ago to see Mr. Bright, and he spent two of the pleasantest hours he ever spent in his life in Mr. Bright's dining-room, listening to him. lie had al- ways admired Mr. Bright, and looked upon him as a great and good man. (Applause.) He thought more of him when he came out of that room than ever he did before, and they might be sure that they did not forget Ireland. (Hear, hear.) lie got Mr. Bright to tell him what he thought about Ireland, the Irish people, and an Irish Parliament, and he could tell them that he came away stronger in his opinion than when he went. (Ap- plause.) They might say what they liked, but there was nobody but their great leader, Mr. Glad- stone—(applause)—that had produced a measure for the settlement of the Irish difficulty that the Irish people and the Irish representatives were satisfied with. (Applause ) Mr. Gladstone's bill was the only one that the Irish representatives had said they would be satisfied with, and that bill of Mr. Gladstone's, or a bill on the same lines, would have to be passed. (Hear, hear, and applause.) He was very sorry that their Liberal party did not all agree upon that question. He respected Lord Hart- ington, Mr. Chamberlain, and Sir Henry James. They were all able, clever, and conscientious men, but for all that they could not wait for them. (Hear, hear.) If they did not choose to come along with them they must go on without them. (Hear, hear.) But they would all see for themselves that Mr. Chamberlain was coming nearer —a good deal nearer that he was six months ago. (Hear, hear.) He thought something would come out of that round table yet. (Laughter, and hear, hear.) At this point, the attention of the Chairman was called by Mr. H. Roberts to the fact that a reporter of the Liverpool Tory newspaper was present, and he was asked if he ruled that the reporter should remain, the Council meeting being a strictly private one, although the reporters of one or two Liberal newspapers were sometimes admitted as a matter of privilege.—The Chairman, after some hubbub, ruled that as two reporters were present, the other should be allowed to remain in the room. Mr. CROSFIELD, resuming, said he did not care if all the Tory reporters in England were present; he never said anything he was ashamed of. (HPar, hear.) They were all aware, he added, that he was goino, on a trip with Alderman Davies. They sailed the following Saturday, and they should not be' back till the 27th April. During the trip he might

div.head: IRISI NATION A L LF, GITE.
div.p: IRISI NATION A L LF, GITE.

- - A meeting of the Warrington branch of the Irish National League was held in the meeting room in Orford-street, on Sunday afternoon, to hear an address by Mr. George Collins, of Liverpool: The chair was occupied by Mr. Chambers. vice-president and there was a a.,00d attendance of members. The Chairman, who was well received, explained that the president (Mr. F. Loughlin) was unavoid- bly not able to be present. He, with very little pre- face, called upon Mr. Collins to address the meet-

ing. Mr. Collins in the course of his speech, said that they believed that the country which gave them birth was prepared to accept, and accept definitely, nothing less, however much more it might accept, than Home Rule forlreland as laid down by Mr. Gladstone's Bill (bear bear.) If there was one thing more than another about which it was safe to say that the whole civilised world, and all faithful thinkers, ware agreed on, it was that, ordinarily speaking, a community w ,uld get on better when it managed its own affairs than when its affairs were wan- aged by another community (cheers). Under the latter con- dition public spirit, self reliance, national faith, national hope, and national charity, wonld decline. Was not that the case of the people who lived within the four seas of Ireland? A large and intelligent community, geographically, his. torically, and actually distinct, were not allowed the management of their own affairs. It was true that they had a small voice in the management of their affairs.l but they had nothing more, for the ultimate control of the domestic concerns of Ireland rested with Eng- land. How could any calm inquirer of the truth resist the conclusion that it would be desirable to revert to the natural order of things, and to give to a distinct and in- telligent community the right to manar.e their own affairs. To a community, as to a man, liberty urea the first of prac- tical advantages, without which energy flagged, and national life itself would decay. Subj•ction was a constant irritant, it caused feuds eng-ndered passion, intensified hate, and lowered self respect. (Cheers) History taught that communi,ies thrived with freedom, and deteriorated under subjection. (Cheers.) That was the general principle which uncrerlay the therry of Home Rule for Ireland, and for all portions of the kingdom. Upon the ground of general principle, he maintained, Ire- land bad proved that her right to Home Rule was strong and straight, and could not be disturbed. (Cheers.) Can- ada bad got Home Rule, America had fought and gained it, and even the Isle of Man, with its 60,000 of population, had the power of governing itself. He vigorously repudiated the statements of Tories an Unionists that Home Rule for Ire- land would mean disintegration of the Empire. It would, on the contrary, make of Ireland a peaceful and prosperous country, and of Britain a greater, stronger, and mightier power than ever she had been before. Mr. Collins spoke at length on the attitude of Mr. Chambeolain in regard to the question most important to Irishmen, and criticised in severe terms the policy of that gent'ethan. Proceeding, he said that whether or not they obtained Home Rule for Ire- land, it was certain that they would not get coercion, for the Irish representatives in the English Parliament had made that impossible. What Irishmen Raked for now they had asked for for eighty years, net as a gift, but as art inalienable right. In a country governed by its own laws, the shameful evictions at Glenbeigh would have been impossible. Since the Land Act of 1881 was passed no less than 70,000 evictions had taken place in Ire- land because the land would set yield the rent. There was no country easier to rule than Ireland would be under fair conditions, but under the present state of affairs there was no country that would be more difficult to manage. (Cheers.) —Mr. WHITBREAD, in proposing a vote of thanks to the speaker, referred to the published statement af the probabi- lity of Sir Gilbert Greenall being raised to the reerage. If that took place there would be another election in Warring- ton, and it was important that they should be up and doing. Out of a voting list of about (1,000 they had about 1,000 Irish votes, .md abey must take care that those votes were used in the right eirection.—Mr. Joni; Criettritas sedonded the resolution. He urged that Irishmen should have liberty to control their internal affairs • that they were entitled to, and that they would have. (Cheers.)—The vote of thanks was then passed, and acknowledged by Mr. Collins.—Mr. P. O'BRIEN proposed a vote of thanks to the Chairman, which, having been seconded by Mr. WHITEHEAD, was cor- dially carried, and the meeting terminated.

Sir Walter Bartelott, M.P., is prevented_by severe illness from attending to his parliamentary duties. It is announced that Lord Dunraven's resignation of the office of Under Secretary for the Colonies has been ac- cepted. He is understoral to take sides with Lord R. Churchill. The new Town Hall at Birkenhead, which has cost £85,000, and is sale to form the fined pile of civic buildings in Cheshire. was opened on Thursday morning by Mr. John Laird, ex-Mayor of Birkenhead. Mr. Labonrcbere, M.P., on Wednesday, opened the North Kensington Liberal Club in Ladbroke-grove, and afterwards addressed a crowded meeting at the Bort:m.7 Schools, Not- ting-hill-eate, on the position,of tlie Liberal 'Arty and the Irish queetion.

div.p: DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS.

Tbe dehate-oniice-i-d&Ss -w-atT resumed- by Mr. SEXTON, who justified the combination called the plan of campaign, and said the reason such combination was not denounced in the Queen's Speech was because it was known to be beyond the reach of the law. He further insisted it was a necessary combination, and being so, it could not be immoral.— Mr. MarrgEws (Home Secretary) said Mr. Parnell's amendment censured the Government for not proposing a measure in the direction of Home Rule; but the present Parliament and Government were pledged and commissioned to refuse it. He called on the House to support the Go• vernment in the endeavour to prevent the spread of an organised combination to defeat the law.—Colonel NoLaw supported the amendment, and Mr. YEREURCIEI condemned the plan of campaign as illegal.—The debate was continued by Mr C S Parker, Mr Lambert, Sir M H Beach, and Mr Healy, after which the Honse divided, there b-ing For the amendment 246 Against 352
Majority The Rouse adjourned at 1-25.

div.head: WIDNIS AND THE QUEEN'S n, JUBILEE.
div.p: WIDNIS AND THE QUEEN'S n, JUBILEE.

A meeting of the committee appointed by the ratepayers to consider in what mode, if any, the Jubilee of the Queen's reign shall be cele- brated at Widnes, met at Alforde Cham- bers on Tuesday afternoon. ,'There were present the Rev. J. Wright Williams, Messrs. F. H. Gossage, J.P., T. Handley, W. W. Gossage, J. Midwood, 11. W. Deacon, E. Carey, F. Heyes, J. Taylor. J. Houghton, and S. Sadler, with J. T. Allen (clerk to the Local Board.) Mr. F. 11. Gossage was appointed chair- man.— Mr. H. W. Deacon inquired what they were expected to do, and the Chairman replied to receive suggestions on recommendation. They were in a very chaotic condition at present.—Mr. Taylor said there did not seem to be any life in the work. There was only one person present not a member of the Local Board. There dud not seem to be much fervour in the proceedings either outside or inside. —The Chairman said the committee was very much too large to do any work. It ought to be "whittled" down. Mr. Allen read a letter from the Rev. James Clarke, who hoped something should be done locally to celebrate the Jubilee. Letters were also read from Mr. J. Brock, J.P., Mr. Thomas Snape, and Major Cross stating their inability to be present at that afternoon's meeting. A long pauSe now ensued, and at length the chairman said it was for them to do what business they thought fit.—A start was made by the chair- man proposing that Mr. Allen be asked to be the hon. sec., and Mr. Deacon seconded the motion, which was carried unanimously. —Mr. Deacon moved that the chairman should act as treasurer, as well as chairman, and that a committee consisting of the chairman, the treasurer, and the secretary, be appointed to consider the whole question and report. (Laughter.)—The Chairman said that was the most "one man " committee he ever heard of. (Laughter.) He declined to accept the treasurership. —On the proposition of Mr. T. Handley, it was re- solved that Mr. Dun, of Parr's Bank, treasurer to the Board, be asked to accept the post.— The Chairman said he was quite open to acknow- ledge that he called the meeting of ratepayers, as he considered under a command from very high authority, as the representative of the Local Board. He was not in accord with having anything to do with the Jubilee in Widnes at all. He had no desire to do anything in the matter whatever. All that wanted doing in the town could be done by the Local Board out of the rates, and then all the people, such as the London and North-Western Railway Co., the Cheshire Lines Committee, and the various limited liability companies in the town from whom they could not obtain any voluntary subscriptions would have to pay their fair share.— Mr. Carey: Still, I suppose you don't object to the idea of having a collection, be it a large or small one for some object or objects outside the ',ewers of the Local Board.—The Chairman : No. I only spoke as an individual and gave my reasons for call- ing the meeting.—Mr. Carey asked would the "Com- mittee like to increase the size and effi- ciency of the Free Library more liberally than a penny rate imould do it This had been suggested, but his impression was that it would be better to wait and see how the library was appreciated.—The Rev. J. Wright Williams said he was ignorant of what objects could be assisted by the rates. He thoroughly appreciated, however, the chairman's remarks that very large companies in Widnes would only help the welfare of the town to the extent of the rates. A conversation ensued, during which various sug- gestions were mooted. Mr. Carey mentioned open spaces as a matter that could be taken up by the Local Board.—The Vicar remarked: that one of the greatest things that could be done as a jubilee memorial would be to inarease the cleanli- ness of the streets by the employment of more scavengers, and also have Waterloo-road better lighted.—The Chairman said if Mr. Williams would make a complaint to the Local Board he could as- sure him it would receive consideration.—Mr. W. H. Deacon suggested the establishment of alms houses for old poor people.—Mr. W. J. Moreland ' wrote stating that it was desirable to incorporate it with the outlying districts, and then the town would be represented by a Mayor in the forthcoming jubilations.—The Chairman said as that far as a park was concerned, it could be carried out by the rates, and he did not , think they would vet a meeting to sanction the expenditure of £2o,ooo.—Mr. Beach said consider-
